disease.name: Indigestion (Dyspepsia)
disease.scientific_name: Dyspepsia / Functional Dyspepsia / Non-Ulcer Dyspepsia / Gastric Dyspepsia
disease.icd_10_code: K30 (Functional dyspepsia); K21.0 (Gastro-oesophageal reflux with oesophagitis); K21.9 (Gastro-oesophageal reflux without oesophagitis); K25 (Gastric ulcer); K26 (Duodenal ulcer); K27 (Peptic ulcer, unspecified); K29.3 (Alcoholic gastritis); K29.7 (Gastritis, unspecified); B96.81 (Helicobacter pylori as the cause of disease classified elsewhere); R10.1 (Pain localised to upper abdomen — epigastric)
disease.category: Gastroenterology / Upper Gastrointestinal Disease / Functional Gastrointestinal Disorder

overview.description: Dyspepsia — commonly known as indigestion — is a clinical syndrome defined by chronic or recurrent discomfort or pain centred in the upper abdomen (epigastrium), frequently including a constellation of symptoms such as epigastric pain or burning, postprandial fullness and heaviness, early satiety (feeling full after eating very little), nausea, belching, and bloating. Dyspepsia is one of the most prevalent gastrointestinal complaints globally, affecting 20-30% of the general population, and accounts for approximately 3-5% of all primary care consultations. It is broadly categorised as either organic dyspepsia (caused by identifiable structural or biochemical pathology — such as peptic ulcer disease, Helicobacter pylori gastritis, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, or gastric cancer) or functional dyspepsia (no organic cause identified despite investigation — approximately 70% of cases). The distinction between these two forms requires clinical assessment, H. pylori testing, and in appropriate cases, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy. Critically, certain symptom patterns called 'alarm features' or 'red flags' — including unexplained weight loss, dysphagia, progressive vomiting, iron-deficiency anaemia, or haematemesis — indicate potentially serious underlying pathology and mandate urgent endoscopic investigation. In India, Helicobacter pylori infection is ubiquitous (prevalence ~70-80%) and is a major driver of dyspepsia, peptic ulcer disease, and gastric cancer; its eradication is a critical public health and clinical priority.
overview.affected_organ: Primarily the upper gastrointestinal tract: stomach (gastric body, antrum, pylorus), duodenum, and distal oesophagus; overlapping with gallbladder, pancreas, and small intestine in differential diagnosis
overview.prevalence: Dyspepsia affects 20-30% of adults globally; approximately 30% of adults in India experience dyspepsia regularly; accounts for 3-5% of all GP consultations; 70% of dyspepsia presentations are functional (no organic cause found at endoscopy); annual cost of dyspepsia management in high-income countries exceeds £500 million (UK alone). H. pylori, the most important single identifiable cause, infects ~70-80% of the Indian population.
overview.age_group: All ages, though most common in adults 25-60 years; new-onset dyspepsia over age 55 is a red flag requiring urgent investigation; H. pylori acquired in childhood in most Indian cases; elderly patients have higher risk of organic causes (cancer, NSAID ulcers)
overview.is_contagious_note: Dyspepsia itself is not contagious; however, H. pylori (a major cause) is transmitted person-to-person via fecal-oral route and may spread within households
overview.is_curable_note: Functional dyspepsia has no single cure but symptoms can be fully controlled with appropriate treatment in the majority of patients. Organic dyspepsia caused by H. pylori is curable with eradication therapy. NSAID-induced dyspepsia resolves on stopping the offending drug.
overview.is_chronic_note: Functional dyspepsia is a chronic condition with waxing-and-waning symptoms over years; organic causes (ulcer, H. pylori) are treatable and potentially curable
overview.key_fact: Up to 70% of Indians are infected with H. pylori — a bacterium that is the single most important preventable cause of peptic ulcer disease and gastric cancer globally. A simple urea breath test can detect it and a 10-14 day antibiotic course can eradicate it — potentially preventing a lifetime of dyspepsia and reducing gastric cancer risk.

types.name: Functional Dyspepsia (FD)
types.description: The most common form — affecting approximately 70% of all patients with dyspepsia. Defined by the Rome IV criteria as the presence of bothersome postprandial fullness, early satiation, epigastric pain, or epigastric burning for at least 3 days per week, over the past 3 months, with symptom onset at least 6 months before diagnosis, in the absence of any organic, systemic, or metabolic disease that would likely explain the symptoms (i.e., upper GI endoscopy is NORMAL or shows only H. pylori gastritis). Functional dyspepsia is a genuine disorder of gut-brain interaction (DGBI) — not a diagnosis of exclusion or 'all in the head'; it involves real abnormalities in gastric motility, visceral sensation, mucosal immune function, and microbiota-gut-brain axis signalling.

rome_iv_criteria.symptoms: One or more of: postprandial fullness; early satiation; epigastric pain; epigastric burning
rome_iv_criteria.duration: Symptoms present for ≥3 months with onset ≥6 months before diagnosis
rome_iv_criteria.exclusion: No organic, systemic, or metabolic disease likely to explain symptoms on routine investigation

subtypes.description: Meal-induced dyspeptic symptoms — the most common FD subtype. Characterised by: bothersome postprandial fullness after ordinary-sized meals; and/or early satiation that prevents finishing a regular meal. Supportive features: upper abdominal bloating; postprandial nausea; excessive belching. Pathophysiology: impaired gastric accommodation (the normal fundal relaxation to receive a meal does not occur — reduced fundic compliance); delayed gastric emptying in some patients; abnormal duodenal lipid and acid sensitivity.
subtypes.symptoms: Fullness and heaviness after eating; feeling stuffed; early satiation; meal-induced nausea; postprandial bloating
subtypes.triggers: Large fatty meals; rich food; lying down after eating; eating too quickly

subtypes.description: Intermittent epigastric pain or burning NOT exclusively associated with meals — may be relieved OR worsened by eating; not relieved by defaecation or passage of flatus (distinguishing from IBS). Characterised by: epigastric pain (at least moderate severity, at least once per week); and/or epigastric burning. Pathophysiology: central and peripheral sensitisation of gastric afferent nociceptors — visceral hypersensitivity (the stomach is more sensitive to normal volumes, distension, and acid); altered brain-gut signalling.
subtypes.symptoms: Burning epigastric pain or discomfort; intermittent; not necessarily meal-related; may occur fasting
subtypes.note: PDS and EPS frequently overlap — up to 50% of FD patients have features of both

pathophysiology_mechanisms: Impaired gastric accommodation — reduced fundal relaxation to receive meals; 30-40% of FD patients; contributes to early satiety, postprandial fullness, nausea
Delayed gastric emptying — 25-35% of FD patients have objective delay on scintigraphy; correlates with postprandial fullness and nausea; more common in female FD patients
Duodenal hypersensitivity to acid and lipids — abnormal afferent signalling from duodenal acid-sensitive receptors; triggers nausea, pain, delayed gastric emptying
Visceral hypersensitivity (central sensitisation) — lower pain threshold to gastric balloon distension; magnified perception of normal physiological events; important in EPS
Duodenal mucosal immune activation — mild eosinophilia and mast cell infiltration in duodenal mucosa of FD patients; low-grade inflammation disrupting mucosal barrier and afferent nerve function
H. pylori-related FD — H. pylori gastritis fulfils Rome IV FD criteria; H. pylori eradication alleviates symptoms in ~10-15% beyond placebo, making it a minor organic component
Gut microbiome dysbiosis — altered duodenal and gastric microbiome composition; reduced Lactobacillus; increased gram-negative bacteria; contributes to mucosal inflammation and motility abnormalities

Gut-brain axis dysregulation — psychological factors (anxiety, depression, early life adversity) alter autonomic nervous system tone and corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF) signalling — directly affects gastric motility and sensory thresholds

Post-infectious FD — 10-15% of FD cases develop after an acute gastroenteritis (post-infectious FD); Giardia, Salmonella, norovirus can trigger persistent FD symptoms through mucosal immune activation
types.prognosis: Chronic and relapsing-remitting; most patients have persistent symptoms for years but with fluctuating severity; approximately 50% have symptom improvement at 12 months with appropriate management; does not progress to cancer or serious disease; quality of life can be significantly impaired

types.name: H. pylori-Associated Dyspepsia and Gastritis
types.description: Helicobacter pylori is a Gram-negative, microaerophilic, spiral-shaped bacterium that colonises the gastric mucosa — the most prevalent chronic bacterial infection globally and classified as a WHO Group 1 carcinogen (definite human carcinogen). H. pylori infects approximately 70-80% of India's population — acquired almost universally in childhood through fecal-oral transmission in conditions of overcrowding and poor sanitation. H. pylori causes chronic active gastritis in ALL infected individuals (though most are asymptomatic); it is the primary cause of peptic ulcer disease, gastric cancer (adenocarcinoma), and gastric MALT lymphoma. When dyspeptic symptoms are present in H. pylori-infected individuals, a 'test-and-treat' strategy is the first-line approach recommended by all major international and Indian guidelines.
types.epidemiology: H. pylori infects 70-80% of Indians; most commonly acquired in childhood (contaminated water, food, person-to-person); higher prevalence in: lower socioeconomic groups, rural areas, overcrowded households; India has one of the highest H. pylori prevalence rates globally; paradoxically, India also has a relatively low gastric cancer rate compared to East Asian countries (the 'Indian enigma' — possibly related to dietary factors and different H. pylori virulence strains)
types.virulence_factors: CagA (cytotoxin-associated gene A) — most important virulence determinant; CagA-positive strains more strongly associated with peptic ulcer and gastric cancer; VacA (vacuolating cytotoxin A) — disrupts gastric epithelium; OipA, BabA, SabA — outer membrane proteins mediating mucosal adhesion
h_pylori_disease_spectrum: Chronic active gastritis — universal; most asymptomatic
Peptic ulcer disease — duodenal ulcer (15-20% of infected); gastric ulcer (5-10% of infected); H. pylori causes 90% of duodenal ulcers and 75% of gastric ulcers
Functional dyspepsia — H. pylori gastritis without ulcer, causing dyspeptic symptoms
Gastric adenocarcinoma (gastric cancer) — 1-3% lifetime risk in infected; H. pylori causes ~89% of non-cardia gastric cancers
Gastric MALT lymphoma (Mucosa-Associated Lymphoid Tissue) — rare; H. pylori eradication achieves complete remission in ~80% of early localised gastric MALT lymphoma

Extragastric manifestations: iron deficiency anaemia (H. pylori reduces non-haem iron absorption); idiopathic thrombocytopaenic purpura (ITP — H. pylori eradication may increase platelet count); Vitamin B12 deficiency (from gastric atrophy)
types.transmission: Fecal-oral (primary — contaminated water, unwashed food); oral-oral (saliva sharing — common in India — sharing food, drinking water vessels); iatrogenic (contaminated endoscopes historically)

types.name: Peptic Ulcer Disease (PUD) — Gastric and Duodenal Ulcers
types.description: Peptic ulcers are breaks in the gastroduodenal mucosa extending through the muscularis mucosae — caused by an imbalance between aggressive factors (gastric acid, pepsin, H. pylori, NSAIDs) and defensive factors (mucus layer, bicarbonate secretion, prostaglandins, mucosal blood flow, mucosal cell renewal). Duodenal ulcers (DU) are far more common than gastric ulcers (GU) in India; DU typically occurs in the 30-50 year age group; both H. pylori (primary cause) and NSAIDs (second most common cause) are major aetiological factors.

types_of_peptic_ulcer.features: Located in the first part of the duodenum (duodenal cap/bulb); pain classically: epigastric, burning, worse at night (wakes patient from sleep), relieved by food or antacids ('hunger pain'); H. pylori positive in ~90%; hypersecretion of gastric acid; rarely malignant (unlike gastric ulcer); occurs in younger adults
types_of_peptic_ulcer.complications: Haemorrhage (20% of DU — haematemesis or melaena); perforation (5% — sudden severe 'board-like' abdominal pain); gastric outlet obstruction (pyloric stenosis from periulcer oedema or fibrosis)

types_of_peptic_ulcer.features: Located in the gastric body or antrum; pain: epigastric, burning, often worsened by food (unlike DU — food-provoked pain); H. pylori positive in ~75%; NSAIDs are important cause; ALWAYS biopsy gastric ulcers at endoscopy to exclude malignancy (even apparently benign-appearing); repeat endoscopy after 6-8 weeks to confirm healing
types_of_peptic_ulcer.complications: Haemorrhage; perforation; malignant transformation (rare — <1% of gastric ulcers are initially malignant but biopsy all)

types.nsaid_induced_ulcer: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, diclofenac, aspirin, naproxen, indomethacin) inhibit COX-1 enzyme — depleting gastroprotective prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2) that normally maintain gastric mucus secretion, bicarbonate production, and mucosal blood flow. NSAID-induced mucosal injury ranges from superficial erosions to full-thickness peptic ulcers. Risk: 15-25% of chronic NSAID users develop peptic ulcers; most are gastric (vs H. pylori which more commonly causes duodenal). Risk factors: age >65, prior ulcer history, high NSAID dose, concomitant corticosteroids or anticoagulants. Prevention: add PPI (omeprazole 20 mg) to any patient on NSAIDs at high ulcer risk.

types.name: Gastro-Oesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) — Overlapping with Dyspepsia
types.description: GERD is caused by abnormal retrograde flow of gastric contents (acid, pepsin, bile) into the oesophagus from failure of the lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) — causing heartburn (pyrosis — burning behind the sternum radiating upward), acid regurgitation (sour taste in mouth, especially on bending or lying), and sometimes water brash (excessive salivation). GERD frequently overlaps with dyspepsia — up to 40% of dyspepsia patients have significant GERD components. Distinguished from pure dyspepsia by the predominance of heartburn and regurgitation (postprandial, lying supine, bending forward) vs epigastric pain and fullness. Chronic untreated GERD leads to oesophagitis, Barrett's oesophagus (precancerous change), oesophageal stricture, and oesophageal adenocarcinoma.
types.prevalence: Affects 20-30% of Western populations; 7-14% of Indian adults; rising prevalence with westernisation of diet and increasing obesity in India
types.risk_factors: Obesity (most important modifiable risk — abdominal fat increases intra-abdominal pressure); pregnancy; hiatus hernia (stomach herniating through oesophageal hiatus); smoking; alcohol; large fatty meals; lying down after eating; coffee and tea; chocolate; mint; tight clothing; certain medications (nitrates, calcium channel blockers, theophylline — relax LOS)
types.alarm_sign_gerd: Dysphagia (difficulty swallowing) in a GERD patient = urgent endoscopy to exclude oesophageal stricture, rings, or cancer; unexplained weight loss with GERD = urgent investigation

types.name: Drug-Induced Dyspepsia
types.description: A very common but frequently overlooked cause of dyspepsia — accounting for up to 25% of chronic dyspepsia in elderly patients on multiple medications. Upper GI irritation from medications is particularly important in India where NSAIDs (diclofenac, ibuprofen, aspirin) and traditional herbal preparations are widely used without adequate gastric protection.

major_causative_drugs.mechanism: COX-1 inhibition depletes prostaglandins — impairs mucosal defence; direct topical irritation
major_causative_drugs.prevalence: Most common drug cause; 30-40% of NSAID users have dyspepsia
major_causative_drugs.management: Lowest effective NSAID dose; switch to COX-2 selective NSAID (celecoxib) if available; add PPI co-prescription

major_causative_drugs.mechanism: Inhibit prostaglandin synthesis; increase acid secretion; synergistic ulcerogenic effect with NSAIDs
major_causative_drugs.management: PPI gastroprotection for anyone on corticosteroids >4 weeks; never give oral steroids + NSAIDs without PPI cover

major_causative_drugs.mechanism: Direct oesophageal and gastric mucosal irritation from tablet formulation
major_causative_drugs.management: Take with full glass of water; remain upright for 30-60 minutes after dosing; PPI if persistent symptoms; consider weekly or monthly dosing (vs daily)

major_causative_drugs.mechanism: Direct gastric mucosal irritation from ferrous iron; nausea, epigastric pain, constipation
major_causative_drugs.management: Take with food (reduces absorption slightly but improves tolerance); switch to ferric iron (less GI irritation); reduce dose and titrate up; take every other day

major_causative_drugs.mechanism: Direct gastric irritation; alteration of gastric motility (erythromycin — motilin receptor agonist causes nausea and cramping)
major_causative_drugs.management: Take with food; switch to alternative antibiotic if possible

major_causative_drugs.mechanism: GI intolerance in 30% of patients initiating metformin — nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, metallic taste
major_causative_drugs.management: Take with food; start at low dose (500 mg once daily) and titrate slowly; switch to extended-release (XR) formulation — significantly reduces GI side effects

major_causative_drugs.mechanism: Highly irritating to gastric and oesophageal mucosa
major_causative_drugs.management: Modified-release or effervescent formulation; always take with plenty of water

major_causative_drugs.mechanism: Narrow therapeutic index drug; GI toxicity (nausea, vomiting, anorexia) is an early sign of toxicity
major_causative_drugs.management: Check digoxin levels; ensure not toxic range

major_causative_drugs.mechanism: Phosphodiesterase inhibitor causing nausea, vomiting, and GI upset; also relaxes lower oesophageal sphincter worsening GERD
major_causative_drugs.management: Check serum levels; dose reduction; use as last-resort bronchodilator

types.name: Gastroparesis
types.description: Delayed gastric emptying in the absence of mechanical obstruction — a specific cause of dyspepsia that is increasingly recognised, particularly in diabetics. The stomach fails to empty its contents normally despite the pylorus being patent, causing chronic symptoms of fullness, nausea, vomiting of undigested food hours after eating, and weight loss. Gastroparesis is a chronic, debilitating condition requiring specialist gastroenterology management.
causes: Diabetic gastroparesis — most common secondary cause; autonomic neuropathy from longstanding poorly controlled diabetes damages the vagal nerve and enteric nervous system (Cajal interstitial cells) controlling gastric peristalsis; affects 30-50% of patients with longstanding type 1 and type 2 diabetes
Post-surgical gastroparesis — after vagotomy (no longer common), gastric bypass, Nissen fundoplication (surgery for GERD)
Idiopathic — most common overall; often post-viral (post-infectious gastroparesis after viral gastroenteritis); predominantly young women
Parkinson's disease — alpha-synuclein deposition in enteric nervous system
Scleroderma and autoimmune connective tissue diseases
Medications — opioids (most important drug cause; severe constipation + gastroparesis); anticholinergics; GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide, exenatide — increasingly important)
types.diagnosis: Gastric emptying scintigraphy (nuclear medicine — 4-hour solid meal study) — gold standard; wireless motility capsule; gastric emptying breath test (non-radioactive C-13 octanoic acid)
types.management: Glycaemic control (optimal blood glucose essential — acute hyperglycaemia further slows gastric emptying); dietary modification (small, frequent, low-fat, soft meals); prokinetics (metoclopramide, domperidone, erythromycin, prucalopride); antiemetics; surgical (gastric electrical stimulation for refractory cases)

types.name: Dyspepsia from Biliary and Pancreatic Disease
types.description: Upper abdominal discomfort from gallbladder disease (cholelithiasis — gallstones, cholecystitis) and pancreatic disease (chronic pancreatitis, pancreatic cancer) can mimic dyspepsia. These must be excluded in patients with dyspepsia, especially those with features of biliary pain (right upper quadrant, radiating to right shoulder, associated with fatty food intake, intermittent and severe — biliary colic) or those not responding to standard dyspepsia treatment.
types.biliary_dyspepsia: Gallstone-related symptoms: right upper quadrant or epigastric pain post-fatty meals; nausea; diagnosis: abdominal ultrasound (investigation of choice); treatment: cholecystectomy for symptomatic gallstones
types.chronic_pancreatitis: Central or left-sided epigastric pain radiating to back; worse after eating; alcohol history; malabsorption (steatorrhoea); diagnosis: CT abdomen, faecal elastase; treatment: enzyme replacement, pain management, alcohol cessation

severity_levels.name: Mild Dyspepsia
severity_levels.description: Occasional or intermittent upper GI symptoms that are manageable with lifestyle modification and over-the-counter medications. Does not significantly impair daily activities or quality of life.
severity_levels.criteria: Symptoms occur less than 3 times per week; symptoms triggered by identifiable dietary or lifestyle factors; no alarm features; no significant weight loss; able to eat normal diet with modification; NRS pain score 1-3/10; no nocturnal symptoms
severity_levels.functional_impact: Mild inconvenience; does not limit activities; able to work and socialise normally
severity_levels.management: Lifestyle modification (smaller meals, avoid triggers, reduce alcohol and caffeine); antacids (Gelusil, Digene, Tums, ENO) as needed; avoid NSAIDs; review and remove precipitating medications; OTC H2 blocker (famotidine) as needed; trial of dietary changes for 2-4 weeks before seeking medical review
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Symptoms worsening or occurring daily; weight loss; no improvement after 4 weeks of lifestyle changes; any alarm features appearing

severity_levels.name: Moderate Dyspepsia
severity_levels.description: Frequent and bothersome upper GI symptoms occurring most days, significantly affecting quality of life, eating habits, and social functioning, but without alarm features.
severity_levels.criteria: Symptoms 3 or more days per week; affects food choices and meal enjoyment; interferes with work or social activities; nocturnal symptoms possible; NRS pain score 4-6/10; no weight loss exceeding 3 kg; no alarm features
severity_levels.functional_impact: Noticeably impairs quality of life; modifies eating habits and social dining; may affect work performance; anxiety about symptoms
severity_levels.management: GP review; H. pylori testing (urea breath test or stool antigen test) — test and treat strategy; empirical PPI trial (omeprazole 20 mg once daily for 4-8 weeks) if H. pylori negative; dietary review with dietitian; stress management; prokinetic if postprandial symptoms dominant
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Any alarm features; failure to respond to H. pylori eradication + PPI therapy; unexplained weight loss; new dysphagia

severity_levels.name: Severe or Refractory Dyspepsia
severity_levels.description: Daily and severe upper GI symptoms significantly impairing quality of life and function, not responding to first-line therapy, or associated with psychological comorbidities.
severity_levels.criteria: Daily symptoms; significantly impairs daily function; NRS pain score 7-9/10; not responding to 8+ weeks of PPI or H. pylori eradication; associated anxiety or depression; weight loss from poor appetite; requires frequent GP or emergency consultations
severity_levels.functional_impact: Significantly reduces quality of life; may cause social withdrawal; high psychological burden; nutritional compromise possible
severity_levels.management: Upper GI endoscopy (if not already performed); specialist gastroenterology review; psychological assessment and management (CBT, hypnotherapy); low-dose tricyclic antidepressant or mirtazapine; prokinetics; buspirone for impaired accommodation; gastric emptying study if gastroparesis suspected
severity_levels.criteria_for_upgrade: Any alarm feature development; significant weight loss; severe vomiting causing dehydration

severity_levels.name: Alarm Features — Urgent Investigation Required
severity_levels.description: Dyspepsia presenting with or developing alarm ('red flag') features that indicate potentially serious underlying pathology — particularly gastric or oesophageal cancer — requiring urgent upper GI endoscopy within 2 weeks.
alarm_features: Unintentional weight loss (>3 kg or >5% body weight over preceding 6 months)
Progressive dysphagia (worsening difficulty swallowing) — suggests oesophageal cancer, stricture, or achalasia
Persistent vomiting — especially large-volume vomiting; vomiting of undigested food hours after eating
Iron-deficiency anaemia without other explanation — possible occult GI blood loss from cancer or ulcer
Haematemesis (vomiting blood — fresh red or coffee-ground) — EMERGENCY — see Red Zone
Melaena (black tarry stools — digested blood) — EMERGENCY
Age >55 years with new onset or recently changed dyspeptic symptoms
Family history of gastric or oesophageal cancer in first-degree relative
Previous gastric surgery or gastric ulcer with new/changed symptoms
Persistent symptoms despite adequate treatment trial (8+ weeks of PPI)
severity_levels.action: Urgent 2-week-wait upper GI endoscopy (OGD/EGD); blood tests (FBC for anaemia, LFTs, albumin, B12, ferritin); CT staging if mass found; urgent gastroenterology referral
severity_levels.note: Absence of alarm features does NOT exclude cancer — alarm features have low sensitivity (30-50%) for detecting cancer; age >55 years with new dyspepsia is an independent indication for endoscopy

causative_agents_overview.h_pylori: Most important identifiable and treatable cause; infects 70-80% of Indians; causes chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer, and gastric cancer; test-and-treat strategy is first-line management
causative_agents_overview.nsaids_aspirin: Second most common cause; direct mucosal injury and prostaglandin depletion; reversible with drug withdrawal; very widely used in India without adequate gastric protection
causative_agents_overview.functional: 70% of dyspepsia after investigation; related to disordered gut-brain interaction, impaired gastric accommodation, visceral hypersensitivity, and gut microbiome dysbiosis
causative_agents_overview.gerd: Acid reflux causing oesophageal and gastric mucosal irritation; frequently overlaps with dyspepsia
causative_agents_overview.medications: NSAIDs, aspirin, oral steroids, bisphosphonates, iron, metformin, antibiotics, opioids
causative_agents_overview.lifestyle: Alcohol, smoking, obesity, stress, dietary excesses (spicy, fatty, acidic foods)

risk_factors: H. pylori infection — dominant risk factor in India; 70-80% population prevalence; acquired in childhood; associated with poverty, crowding, poor sanitation
NSAID and aspirin use — including OTC pain relievers; very common self-medication in India; lack of gastroprotection
Alcohol consumption — direct gastric mucosal irritant; increases gastric acid secretion; worsens GERD
Tobacco smoking — increases gastric acid output; impairs mucosal healing; H. pylori eradication less successful in smokers; slows gastric emptying
Obesity — increases intra-abdominal pressure causing GERD and dyspepsia; associated with delayed gastric emptying
Irregular eating habits — skipping meals; eating very late at night; eating too rapidly; irregular meal timing
Dietary patterns — excessive spicy food; very fatty or fried food; excessive tea and coffee; carbonated beverages; irregular large meals
Psychological stress, anxiety, and depression — bidirectional gut-brain axis; stress directly affects gastric motility, acid secretion, and visceral sensation
Age over 55 years — higher risk of organic pathology (cancer, atrophic gastritis); NSAID use more common
Family history of gastric cancer or peptic ulcer disease — H. pylori familial clustering; genetic predisposition
Diabetes mellitus — gastroparesis; autonomic neuropathy affecting gastric motility
Previous gastric surgery — dumping syndrome; bile reflux gastritis; afferent loop syndrome
Medications — see TYPE-05 above for full list
Low socioeconomic status — H. pylori acquisition; dietary irregularity; delayed care-seeking
Spicy and acidic food overconsumption — particularly in South Indian and street food contexts; capsaicin activates TRPV1 receptors in gastric mucosa directly causing pain and dyspepsia
Late night eating — high acid output at night with food in stomach increases mucosal exposure; gravity-dependent GERD in sleep
Low physical activity — reduced GI motility; obesity; constipation contributing to dyspeptic symptoms

symptoms.overview: Dyspepsia encompasses a spectrum of upper GI symptoms that patients may describe variously as 'gas', 'acidity', 'gastric problem', 'indigestion', 'heaviness after eating', 'burning in stomach', or 'stomach pain'. The key upper abdominal location (epigastrium — below the sternum, above the umbilicus), association with eating, and the specific symptom character are the clinically important features. Patients presenting with these symptoms in India most commonly use the terms 'gas problem', 'acidity', or 'stomach upset'. Understanding the precise symptom pattern — whether meal-related, nocturnal, burning vs cramping, relieved or worsened by eating — guides diagnosis and treatment selection.

primary_symptoms.name: Epigastric Pain or Burning (Heartburn-like)
primary_symptoms.description: Pain or burning discomfort localised to the epigastrium (upper middle abdomen, below the sternum/breastbone) — the cardinal symptom of dyspepsia. Must be distinguished from heartburn (retrosternal burning — behind the sternum) which is more typical of GERD. Epigastric burning in dyspepsia is typically intermittent; may be worsened by food (gastric ulcer) or relieved by food (duodenal ulcer); may be worsened by lying flat (raising suspicion for GERD overlap). Night waking from epigastric pain is characteristic of duodenal ulcer (acid hypersecretion at night unopposed by food buffer).
primary_symptoms.onset: Functional: gradual, recurrent; Peptic ulcer: may be acute; NSAID-induced: onset after starting NSAID
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: Pain that is severe, constant, and radiates to the back suggests pancreatitis; pain with rigidity and rebound tenderness suggests perforation — EMERGENCY

primary_symptoms.name: Postprandial Fullness and Heaviness
primary_symptoms.description: An unpleasant sensation of fullness after eating a normal or even small meal — the stomach feels 'full', 'heavy', 'bloated', or 'distended' long after eating. Caused by impaired gastric accommodation (the normal relaxation of the gastric fundus to receive food does not occur normally) and delayed gastric emptying. Very distressing symptom — prevents patients from enjoying normal meals, affects social eating, and can cause significant weight loss when severe.
primary_symptoms.onset: Typically begins 15-30 minutes after starting to eat
primary_symptoms.associated: Often accompanied by nausea, belching, and upper abdominal distension

primary_symptoms.name: Early Satiation (Early Satiety)
primary_symptoms.description: An abnormally rapid sensation of fullness shortly after starting a meal — the patient cannot eat a normal-sized portion before feeling uncomfortably full. Distinct from postprandial fullness (which comes later); early satiety prevents completing a meal. Results from impaired fundic accommodation and rapid post-meal pressure rise in the gastric fundus. When severe, leads to reduced caloric intake and weight loss. Also a feature of gastroparesis and gastric outlet obstruction.
primary_symptoms.onset: After first few mouthfuls of food
primary_symptoms.note: Persistent early satiety with weight loss is an alarm feature requiring endoscopic investigation

primary_symptoms.name: Nausea
primary_symptoms.description: The sensation of queasiness and the urge to vomit — very common in functional dyspepsia, particularly postprandial distress syndrome. Nausea in dyspepsia is typically triggered or worsened by eating, food smells, or fatty meals. It may prevent eating and contribute to weight loss. Persistent vomiting (vs occasional nausea) is an alarm feature. In gastroparesis: nausea is the dominant symptom; vomiting of undigested food hours after eating is characteristic.
primary_symptoms.note: Vomiting of large volumes of food hours or days after eating = gastroparesis or gastric outlet obstruction — requires investigation

primary_symptoms.name: Bloating and Abdominal Distension
primary_symptoms.description: A sense of excess gas or pressure in the upper abdomen — described as 'gaseous', 'tight', 'distended', or 'full of air'. In Indian culture, 'gas problem' (vaayu) is the most common lay description of dyspepsia. Bloating in dyspepsia is from: aerophagia (excess air swallowing); impaired gas transit through the gut; abnormal visceral sensation (even normal gas volumes feel excessive); bacterial fermentation of undigested carbohydrates. Upper abdominal bloating is more typical of dyspepsia; lower abdominal bloating with change in bowel habit suggests IBS (irritable bowel syndrome).
primary_symptoms.note: Bloating and flatulence are the most common GI symptoms in India and frequently self-treated with Eno, Gelusil, ajwain water, or jeera water before seeking medical consultation

primary_symptoms.name: Belching (Eructation) and Excessive Gas
primary_symptoms.description: Frequent and bothersome passage of gas from the stomach through the mouth — either from aerophagia (swallowing excess air — most common cause) or from postprandial gastric gas production. Supragastric belching (a learned behaviour in which air is injected into the oesophagus and immediately expelled) is a recognised specific belching disorder in Rome IV — characterised by repetitive belching episodes, particularly during stress; not truly from the stomach; requires behavioural therapy (speech therapy/biofeedback) rather than medications.
primary_symptoms.note: Excessive belching is the second most common GI complaint in India after 'gas and acidity'

primary_symptoms.name: Heartburn and Acid Regurgitation (GERD-Overlap Symptoms)
primary_symptoms.description: Heartburn (pyrosis) — burning discomfort rising from the stomach or lower chest toward the throat — is the dominant symptom of GERD but frequently overlaps with dyspepsia. Acid regurgitation — the effortless flow of acidic or bitter fluid into the mouth or throat — also suggests GERD. Water brash (sudden mouth filling with saliva — a reflex response to oesophageal acid exposure) is a specific GERD symptom. When heartburn and regurgitation predominate, the diagnosis is GERD rather than pure dyspepsia — PPIs are the treatment of choice.
primary_symptoms.note: Heartburn that is particularly severe on lying flat, bending forward, or after large fatty meals is typical of GERD

secondary_symptoms: Excessive flatulence (wind) — from fermentation of undigested carbohydrates; common complaint in Indian patients
Appetite loss and food aversion — from early satiety, nausea, and anticipatory anxiety about postprandial symptoms
Metallic or sour taste in mouth — acid reflux reaching the oropharynx
Bad breath (halitosis) — from H. pylori infection; GERD; food stagnation in gastroparesis
Upper abdominal gurgling (borborygmi) — intestinal gas movement; overlaps with IBS
Constipation or altered bowel habit — functional dyspepsia overlaps with IBS in 40% of patients
Fatigue — from chronic pain, poor sleep, anxiety, nutritional inadequacy
Insomnia — from nocturnal acid reflux, pain, or anxiety about symptoms
Anxiety and depression — highly prevalent in FD; bidirectional gut-brain relationship
Weight loss — from reduced food intake from early satiety, nausea, or food aversion (alarm feature if >3 kg unintentional)
red_flags_alarm_features_must_investigat: Unintentional weight loss >3 kg — possible gastric cancer or severe gastroparesis
Progressive difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) — oesophageal cancer, stricture, or achalasia — URGENT endoscopy
Vomiting blood (haematemesis) — bright red or coffee-ground — EMERGENCY
Black tarry stools (melaena) — GI bleeding from ulcer or cancer — EMERGENCY
Iron-deficiency anaemia without other explanation — possible occult GI blood loss
Persistent vomiting preventing adequate nutrition — possible gastric outlet obstruction or gastroparesis
New onset dyspepsia in patient over 55 years — higher cancer risk
Family history of gastric or oesophageal cancer in first-degree relative
Sudden severe 'worst ever' epigastric pain with abdominal rigidity — possible peptic ulcer perforation — SURGICAL EMERGENCY

differentiating_symptoms.duodenal_ulcer: Pain worse at night; hunger pain relieved by food or antacids; epigastric; H. pylori very likely
differentiating_symptoms.gastric_ulcer: Pain worsened by food (food-provoked); weight loss possible; always biopsy to exclude cancer
differentiating_symptoms.gerd: Retrosternal burning; worse lying flat; acid regurgitation; relieved by PPIs
differentiating_symptoms.gastroparesis: Vomiting hours after eating; undigested food; weight loss; diabetes history
differentiating_symptoms.biliary_colic: Severe right upper quadrant pain post-fat meal; radiates to shoulder; spasmodic; not continuous
differentiating_symptoms.pancreatitis: Severe constant epigastric pain radiating to back; worse eating; elevated lipase/amylase; alcohol history
differentiating_symptoms.functional_dyspepsia: Meal-related fullness or intermittent epigastric pain; normal endoscopy; often associated with anxiety/stress

medical_history: Precise symptom characterisation — epigastric pain vs fullness vs nausea vs heartburn vs regurgitation; which symptom predominates (guides subtype: EPS vs PDS vs GERD-overlap)
Onset and duration — acute (days: possible ulcer, gastritis) vs chronic (months-years: functional dyspepsia); first episode vs recurrent
Relationship to food — meal-triggered (PDS, gastroparesis, biliary); empty stomach pain relieved by food (DU); meal-worsened pain (GU); post-fatty meal pain (biliary colic)
Timing — nocturnal symptoms (DU — wakes at night; GERD — lying flat); morning symptoms (coffee/tea-triggered); post-meal timing (within 30 min: PDS; 1-3 hours: possible DU)
Duration and frequency — daily vs episodic; how many days per week
Aggravating and relieving factors — food (type and timing); antacids (relief = acid-related); lying flat (worsens GERD, may relieve DU); physical activity; stress
Alarm features review — weight loss amount and duration; dysphagia; haematemesis or dark stools; anaemia symptoms (breathlessness, fatigue, pallor)
NSAID and aspirin use — type, dose, frequency, duration; over-the-counter use (often not volunteered); corticosteroid use; other listed drugs
H. pylori history — previous testing; previous eradication treatment; family members with peptic ulcer disease or gastric cancer
Alcohol consumption — type, amount, frequency; acute (gastritis) vs chronic (gastric atrophy)
Tobacco use — smoking or chewing tobacco; both worsen dyspepsia and impair H. pylori eradication
Dietary habits — meal timing and size; spicy, fatty, or acidic food intake; tea and coffee; carbonated drinks; late night eating
Occupation and stress levels — work-related stress; shift work (irregular meals); anxiety and depression assessment
Previous investigations — previous OGD (endoscopy), H. pylori test, ultrasound, CT; what were the findings?
Previous treatments — what has been tried? What worked? What didn't? PPIs, antacids, prokinetics; at what dose and duration?
Family history — gastric cancer (first-degree relative = risk factor); peptic ulcer disease; H. pylori eradication in family
Travel history — GERD and dyspepsia prevalence higher in urbanised settings; changes in diet during travel
Relevant medical history — diabetes (gastroparesis risk); thyroid disease (hypothyroidism causes dysmotility); connective tissue disease (scleroderma); previous GI surgery; Crohn's disease
Medications — full medication list including herbal preparations; Ayurvedic medicine; OTC analgesics (important not to miss)
physical_examination: General appearance — weight and BMI (weight loss = alarm); pallor (anaemia from GI bleeding); nutritional status
Vital signs — heart rate (tachycardia in GI haemorrhage); blood pressure (hypotension = haemodynamic compromise from major bleeding)
INSPECTION: visible peristalsis from right to left (visible gastric waves = gastric outlet obstruction — rare but important sign); abdominal distension; surgical scars

PALPATION: epigastric tenderness (most common finding in dyspepsia — non-specific); localised guarding or rigidity (peritonitis — perforation); palpable epigastric mass (gastric cancer, pancreatic mass — alarm sign); succussion splash — patient lying supine, place stethoscope on abdomen, rock patient side to side — splashing sound = fluid in distended stomach (gastric outlet obstruction); Carnett's sign (abdominal wall tenderness worse on tensing abdominal muscles — suggests musculoskeletal pain rather than visceral)
PERCUSSION: gastric tympany (normal); shifting dullness (unusual in dyspepsia — suggests ascites from advanced malignancy)
AUSCULTATION: bowel sounds (absent = ileus or peritonitis; succussion splash — see above)
Rectal examination: stool colour (melaena — black tarry = upper GI bleeding; occult blood testing); palpable mass (unusual)

Signs of systemic disease: jaundice (hepatic disease mimicking dyspepsia); lymphadenopathy — supraclavicular (Virchow's node = gastric cancer metastasis — Troisier's sign); spider naevi, palmar erythema (chronic liver disease)
Skin: pallor of conjunctivae and nail beds (anaemia — iron deficiency from chronic GI blood loss or B12 deficiency from atrophic gastritis)
Hands: Osler's nodes, leukonychia (protein deficiency — chronic disease)

diagnostic_tests.test_name: H. pylori Urea Breath Test (UBT) — Gold Standard Non-Invasive Test
diagnostic_tests.description: The most accurate non-invasive test for detecting active H. pylori infection — the most important initial investigation in all patients with dyspepsia without alarm features. The patient swallows a preparation containing 13C-labelled urea (non-radioactive, safe). If H. pylori is present in the stomach, its urease enzyme breaks down the labelled urea releasing 13CO2 into the bloodstream and expelled in breath — detected by a breath sample analysed by a mass spectrometer. Highly accurate: sensitivity and specificity >95%.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose active H. pylori infection; confirm H. pylori eradication 4-6 weeks after completing treatment (test of cure); preferred over serology (serology remains positive for years after eradication — cannot confirm cure)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive UBT = active H. pylori infection — treat with eradication therapy; Negative UBT = no current H. pylori (though may have been treated and now negative)
diagnostic_tests.preparation: Must stop: PPIs for 2 weeks before testing; H2 blockers for 24-48 hours; antibiotics and bismuth for 4 weeks before testing — otherwise false negative results
diagnostic_tests.india_note: UBT widely available in India at large hospitals and diagnostic centres; cost approximately Rs 500-1,500; ensure patient follows PPI washout instructions; most appropriate initial test for dyspepsia in Indian primary care
diagnostic_tests.test_of_cure: Repeat UBT at least 4 weeks after completing H. pylori eradication therapy (off PPIs for 2 weeks) — ESSENTIAL to confirm successful eradication; do not rely on symptom improvement alone (symptoms may improve even with failed eradication)

diagnostic_tests.description: Monoclonal antibody-based enzyme immunoassay detecting H. pylori antigens in a fresh stool sample. Accuracy comparable to UBT (sensitivity ~94%, specificity ~97%). Increasingly used as an alternative to UBT — cheaper, no equipment needed for the patient (no breath test apparatus), particularly useful in children who cannot cooperate with breath test. Available as ELISA laboratory test or rapid point-of-care immunochromatographic test.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose active H. pylori infection; test of cure (at least 4 weeks after treatment, off PPIs); suitable for children and elderly
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive SAT = active H. pylori — treat; useful also to confirm eradication post-treatment (at least 4 weeks after completing antibiotics, off PPIs for 2 weeks)
diagnostic_tests.preparation: Stop PPIs 2 weeks before; stop antibiotics 4 weeks before; same as UBT

diagnostic_tests.description: Detects IgG antibodies against H. pylori. Less useful than UBT or stool antigen test because: serology remains positive for months to years after successful H. pylori eradication — cannot be used to confirm eradication success; less sensitive (75-85%) and specific (79-90%) than UBT/stool antigen for active infection. Main role: population surveys; low-resource settings where UBT or stool antigen not available; some pre-endoscopy screening.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Limited use — mainly population surveys; not useful for confirming eradication; do not use serology as test of cure
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Positive IgG = past or current infection (cannot distinguish); negative IgG = never infected (in low-prevalence populations) or remote past infection
diagnostic_tests.note: In India where H. pylori prevalence is ~70-80%, a positive serology adds little diagnostic information — almost everyone has been exposed; invest in UBT or stool antigen instead

diagnostic_tests.description: A flexible fibre-optic or video endoscope passed through the mouth, oesophagus, stomach, and duodenum — providing direct visual examination of the upper GI mucosa and the ability to take biopsies. The gold standard investigation for organic causes of dyspepsia: identifies and characterises oesophagitis (GERD-related), peptic ulcers (both gastric and duodenal), gastritis (erythema, erosions, H. pylori changes), oesophageal cancer, gastric cancer, and other pathology. Biopsies are taken from any suspicious lesion, from the antrum and corpus for H. pylori (CLO test — urease rapid test and histology), and from gastric ulcers (mandatory — to exclude malignancy).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose organic dyspepsia; exclude gastric and oesophageal cancer; characterise peptic ulcers; detect Barrett's oesophagus; obtain biopsies for H. pylori (histology and CLO test); monitor gastric ulcer healing
indications: Any ALARM FEATURE present (mandatory urgent investigation)
Age ≥55 years with new onset dyspepsia
Failure to respond to 8 weeks of PPI therapy
Failure of H. pylori eradication to resolve symptoms
Known gastric ulcer — repeat endoscopy after 6-8 weeks treatment to confirm healing and re-biopsy
Chronic NSAID or aspirin use with new symptoms
Patient preference for certainty of diagnosis after full counselling
Pre-bariatric surgery or major upper GI surgery
diagnostic_tests.what_is_found: Normal endoscopy in 70% of dyspepsia patients (= functional dyspepsia diagnosis supported); peptic ulcer in 15-25%; oesophagitis/GERD in 10-20%; cancer in <1% of unselected dyspepsia patients but higher in alarm feature patients
diagnostic_tests.note: Endoscopy WITHOUT alarm features or age >55: reassuringly normal in majority; does not significantly change management in low-risk patients; reserve for indicated cases to avoid unnecessary procedures

diagnostic_tests.test_name: CLO Test (Campylobacter-Like Organism Test — Rapid Urease Test)
diagnostic_tests.description: A rapid point-of-care test performed on gastric biopsy samples taken during endoscopy. A small gastric biopsy (from the antrum or corpus) is placed in a gel containing urea and a pH indicator. If H. pylori is present, its urease enzyme converts urea to ammonia — raising the pH and changing the indicator from yellow to pink/red. Result within 1-3 hours of endoscopy. Used routinely when endoscopy is performed.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Rapid diagnosis of H. pylori at time of endoscopy; biopsy material also sent for histological confirmation
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Pink/red colour change = H. pylori positive; remains yellow = negative; sensitivity 85-98%; specificity 95-100%
diagnostic_tests.preparation: Must stop PPIs 2 weeks and antibiotics 4 weeks before endoscopy to avoid false negative CLO test

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Full Blood Count (FBC) / Complete Blood Count
diagnostic_tests.description: Essential in all new dyspepsia patients. Iron-deficiency anaemia (microcytic, hypochromic — low Hb, low MCV, low ferritin, low serum iron, high TIBC) is an alarm feature suggesting chronic occult GI blood loss from peptic ulcer or cancer. Macrocytic anaemia suggests B12 deficiency — which can result from H. pylori-induced atrophic gastritis (impaired intrinsic factor secretion) or long-term PPI use (PPIs reduce gastric acid, impairing B12 absorption from food). Eosinophilia may suggest eosinophilic gastritis.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for GI blood loss anaemia (alarm feature); detect B12 or folate deficiency; baseline before H. pylori eradication therapy
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Hb <120 g/L women / <130 g/L men = anaemia; MCV <80 fL = microcytic (iron deficiency); MCV >100 fL = macrocytic (B12/folate); ferritin <15 mcg/L = iron deficiency

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Serum Ferritin, Iron Studies, and B12/Folate
diagnostic_tests.description: Ferritin is the gold standard test for iron deficiency (the most sensitive and specific single test). H. pylori reduces non-haem iron absorption from the duodenum and stomach (contributes to iron deficiency even without overt bleeding). Serum B12 deficiency occurs in up to 30% of long-term PPI users (>12 months) and in patients with H. pylori-induced atrophic gastritis. All patients with dyspepsia and unexplained iron deficiency or B12 deficiency should have endoscopy and H. pylori testing.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm iron deficiency (possible alarm feature from occult GI blood loss or H. pylori-related malabsorption); screen for B12 deficiency in long-term PPI users
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Ferritin <15 mcg/L = iron deficient (absolute); Ferritin <30 mcg/L in a symptomatic patient = functional iron deficiency; B12 <200 pg/mL = deficiency

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Liver Function Tests (LFTs), Lipase, Renal Function
diagnostic_tests.description: Part of the workup to exclude hepatic, biliary, and pancreatic causes of upper GI symptoms: elevated bilirubin and transaminases suggest hepatobiliary disease (hepatitis, cholangitis); elevated lipase (preferred over amylase) indicates pancreatitis; elevated ALP suggests biliary pathology. Thyroid function tests (TFTs) are important — hypothyroidism is a common and reversible cause of dysmotility, delayed gastric emptying, nausea, and constipation that can mimic dyspepsia.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude hepatic, pancreatic, and biliary disease mimicking dyspepsia; assess metabolic contributions
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Lipase >3× ULN = pancreatitis; ALT/AST elevation = hepatitis; ALP elevation = biliary disease; TSH elevation = hypothyroidism causing dysmotility

diagnostic_tests.description: First-line imaging investigation for dyspepsia — particularly when: biliary symptoms (right upper quadrant, post-fatty meal); elevated LFTs or ALP (biliary obstruction); epigastric mass; exclusion of other intra-abdominal pathology. Ultrasound identifies: gallstones (cholelithiasis) and cholecystitis; common bile duct dilation; hepatic lesions; pancreatic masses; aortic aneurysm (important differential for epigastric pain). Normal in most functional dyspepsia patients.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Exclude biliary disease (gallstones — most common finding); hepatic and pancreatic pathology; epigastric mass
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Echogenic foci with posterior acoustic shadowing in gallbladder = gallstones; thickened gallbladder wall + pericholecystic fluid = cholecystitis; dilated CBD = biliary obstruction
diagnostic_tests.note: Gallstones are very common (10-15% of adults in India) and frequently incidental — the presence of gallstones does NOT necessarily explain dyspepsia; only symptomatic gallstones (biliary colic) should be treated surgically

diagnostic_tests.description: The gold standard investigation for gastroparesis. Patient eats a standardised meal labelled with a small amount of radioactive isotope (Tc-99m sulphur colloid); a gamma camera measures the rate at which the meal empties from the stomach over 4 hours. Normal: >90% emptied by 4 hours. Delayed gastric emptying at 4 hours = gastroparesis. Required when: suspected gastroparesis (vomiting undigested food, diabetic dyspepsia not responding to standard therapy); unexplained severe early satiety and weight loss; before prokinetic therapy.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose and quantify gastroparesis; guide treatment selection (prokinetics, dietary modification, gastric electrical stimulation)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Gastric retention >10% at 4 hours = gastroparesis; >60% at 2 hours = severe delayed emptying
diagnostic_tests.alternatives: 13C octanoic acid breath test (non-radioactive; available in some Indian centres); wireless motility capsule (SmartPill)

diagnostic_tests.description: A thin probe placed in the oesophagus via the nose records pH over 24 hours, quantifying acid and non-acid reflux events. Combined impedance-pH monitoring detects both acid and weakly acidic (bile reflux) events. The gold standard investigation for diagnosing pathological GERD when endoscopy is normal or inconclusive. Required for: suspected GERD with negative endoscopy; atypical GERD symptoms (chronic cough, laryngitis, hoarseness attributed to reflux); before anti-reflux surgery; refractory symptoms on PPI.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Quantify acid and non-acid reflux exposure; diagnose GERD objectively when clinical diagnosis is uncertain; guide management before anti-reflux surgery
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: DeMeester score >14.72 = pathological acid exposure; acid exposure time (AET) >6% = abnormal; normal acid exposure with symptoms = functional heartburn (acid hypersensitivity)

diagnostic_tests.description: Measures pressure and motility patterns in the oesophagus and lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS). Identifies: achalasia (failure of LOS to relax — causing dysphagia and regurgitation); oesophageal spasm (causing severe chest pain and dysphagia); ineffective oesophageal motility (weakly positive peristalsis — common in GERD). Required before anti-reflux surgery (to ensure adequate peristaltic function) and in unexplained dysphagia.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Assess oesophageal motor function; diagnose achalasia and motility disorders; pre-surgical assessment

medicines.note: The treatment of dyspepsia is targeted to the underlying cause: H. pylori eradication for H. pylori-positive dyspepsia (first-line); acid suppression (PPIs or H2 blockers) for GERD-overlap, peptic ulcer disease, and empirical acid suppression; prokinetics for gastroparesis and postprandial distress syndrome; low-dose antidepressants for refractory functional dyspepsia. Antacids provide symptomatic relief but are not curative. PPI overuse and over-prescription is a major problem in India — PPIs should not be prescribed indefinitely without indication; reassess regularly.
treatment_principles: 1. TEST AND TREAT for H. pylori: all dyspepsia patients without alarm features — test first with urea breath test or stool antigen; if positive, ERADICATE H. pylori before empirical PPI therapy; eradication resolves dyspepsia in 10-15% more patients than placebo and prevents peptic ulcer disease

2. EMPIRICAL PPI TRIAL for 4-8 weeks: appropriate when H. pylori negative, or as initial therapy while awaiting test results; use lowest effective PPI dose; review and reassess at 4-8 weeks — do not continue PPIs indefinitely without indication

3. REVIEW AND STOP NSAIDS: every patient with dyspepsia must have all NSAID and aspirin use reviewed; if NSAIDs essential — add PPI co-prescription; consider switching to paracetamol or COX-2 inhibitor
4. LIFESTYLE MODIFICATION is essential and must precede or accompany pharmacological treatment — dietary changes, meal spacing, weight loss, alcohol and smoking cessation, stress reduction
5. ANTACIDS for immediate symptom relief: appropriate as PRN (as-needed) rescue medication; not appropriate for chronic daily use as monotherapy

6. H. PYLORI ERADICATION — always confirm success with test of cure (UBT or stool antigen at least 4 weeks post-treatment, off PPIs for 2 weeks); resistance rates to clarithromycin and metronidazole are increasing in India — bismuth-based quadruple therapy increasingly preferred
7. PROKINETICS: for gastroparesis and postprandial distress syndrome with prominent fullness, early satiety, and nausea; domperidone or metoclopramide short-term; itopride for longer use

8. LOW-DOSE TRICYCLICS or MIRTAZAPINE: for refractory functional dyspepsia — small doses have central visceral analgesic and anxiolytic effects; start low (amitriptyline 10-25 mg at night); explain rationale clearly to patients (not for depression but for pain modulation)

9. AVOID UNNECESSARY LONG-TERM PPI USE: reassess at every consultation; PPI side effects with long-term use include: C. difficile colitis, community-acquired pneumonia, bone fractures, B12 deficiency, hypomagnesaemia, renal disease, dementia (controversial); step down or stop if no ongoing indication

categories.purpose: Eliminate H. pylori infection from the gastric mucosa — resolves H. pylori gastritis, heals peptic ulcers, prevents ulcer recurrence, reduces gastric cancer risk, and improves dyspepsia symptoms in a subset of patients.
categories.treatment_duration: 10-14 days recommended; 14 days achieves higher eradication rates; do NOT use 7-day regimens (insufficient)

regimens.name: Standard Triple Therapy (First-Line in Low-Clarithromycin-Resistance Areas)
regimens.components: PPI (standard dose twice daily) + Clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily + Amoxicillin 1 g twice daily for 14 days
regimens.brand_examples: PPI: omeprazole 20 mg or pantoprazole 40 mg; Clarithromycin: Clarith, Clar; Amoxicillin: Amoxil, Mox
regimens.use_case: First-line in regions where clarithromycin resistance is <15-20%; appropriate in many parts of India; if penicillin allergy — substitute metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for amoxicillin
regimens.eradication_rate: 70-85% (adequate in low-resistance areas; declining in areas with increasing clarithromycin resistance)
regimens.resistance_concern: Clarithromycin resistance in India rising (15-25% in some centres); H. pylori clarithromycin resistance renders triple therapy ineffective; test for resistance if available or use bismuth quadruple therapy empirically in areas with known high resistance

regimens.name: Bismuth-Based Quadruple Therapy (BQT) — Preferred in India and High-Resistance Areas
regimens.components: PPI (standard dose twice daily) + Bismuth subsalicylate or bismuth subcitrate 120-240 mg four times daily + Tetracycline 500 mg four times daily + Metronidazole 400-500 mg three to four times daily for 10-14 days
regimens.brand_examples: Bismuth subsalicylate: Pepto-Bismol, Bismuth; Tetracycline: Hostacycline, Tetracycline; Metronidazole: Flagyl, Metrogyl
regimens.use_case: Preferred first-line in India given rising clarithromycin resistance; preferred when: previous macrolide antibiotic use; penicillin allergy; known clarithromycin resistance; second-line after triple therapy failure; highly effective even against clarithromycin and metronidazole-resistant strains (bismuth has direct bactericidal activity against H. pylori)
regimens.note: Bismuth salts cause BLACK STOOLS AND TONGUE (benign — harmless bismuth sulphide — reassure patients); tetracycline cannot be used in pregnancy or children <12 years

regimens.name: Sequential Therapy
regimens.components: 5 days: PPI + Amoxicillin 1g twice daily — THEN — 5 days: PPI + Clarithromycin 500 mg twice daily + Metronidazole 400 mg twice daily (total 10 days)
regimens.eradication_rate: 80-90%; slightly superior to standard triple therapy; used in some Indian centres
regimens.note: Less commonly used now that bismuth quadruple therapy is available

regimens.name: Concomitant Therapy
regimens.components: PPI + Amoxicillin 1g + Clarithromycin 500 mg + Metronidazole 400 mg — all taken twice daily together for 10-14 days
regimens.use_case: Alternative to bismuth quadruple when bismuth not available

regimens.name: Second-Line (Salvage) Therapy after Initial Failure
options: Bismuth quadruple therapy (if not used as first-line)
Levofloxacin-based triple therapy: PPI + Levofloxacin 500 mg once daily + Amoxicillin 1g twice daily for 10-14 days
Rifabutin-based therapy: PPI + Rifabutin 300 mg/day + Amoxicillin 1g twice daily (reserved for multiple eradication failures — avoid in TB-endemic area; rifabutin is an anti-TB drug)
regimens.eradication_rate: 60-80% for second-line; after two failures — culture and sensitivity testing strongly recommended
regimens.culture_guidance: H. pylori antimicrobial susceptibility testing should be performed when: two eradication attempts have failed; in populations with high resistance; available in some tertiary centres in India (PCR-based resistance testing increasingly available)

individual_agents.name: Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) — Component of H. pylori Regimens
individual_agents.agents: Omeprazole 20 mg, Pantoprazole 40 mg, Esomeprazole 40 mg, Rabeprazole 20 mg, Lansoprazole 30 mg — all given TWICE daily (not once daily) during H. pylori eradication to maximise acid suppression
individual_agents.note: Rabeprazole may be slightly superior to other PPIs for H. pylori eradication due to less CYP2C19 polymorphism effect; omeprazole and pantoprazole are most widely available generics in India

categories.category_name: Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) — Acid Suppression Therapy
categories.purpose: Suppress gastric acid secretion by irreversibly inhibiting the H+/K+-ATPase proton pump on gastric parietal cells — the most powerful acid-suppressing agents available. First-line for: GERD, peptic ulcer disease, H. pylori eradication (as a component), NSAID gastroprotection, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and empirical acid suppression in dyspepsia.

medicines.name: Omeprazole
medicines.form: Capsule, Tablet (10 mg, 20 mg, 40 mg); IV injection
medicines.dosage: Dyspepsia/GERD: 20 mg once daily (30 min before breakfast for maximum efficacy); Peptic ulcer: 20-40 mg once daily; NSAID prophylaxis: 20 mg once daily; Severe GERD: 40 mg once daily; H. pylori eradication: 20 mg twice daily (as component of triple/quadruple therapy)
medicines.use_case: Most widely prescribed and lowest cost PPI in India; first-line empirical acid suppression for uninvestigated dyspepsia; GERD; peptic ulcer healing; NSAID gastroprotection; component of H. pylori eradication regimens
medicines.mechanism: Prodrug — activated in acidic environment of gastric canaliculi; active form covalently binds and irreversibly inhibits H+/K+-ATPase (proton pump) on parietal cell; reduces gastric acid output by 90-98%; takes 3-5 days to reach maximum effect (new pumps synthesised daily)
medicines.when_to_take: 30-60 MINUTES BEFORE FIRST MEAL OF THE DAY for maximum efficacy — PPIs work only on actively secreting proton pumps which are stimulated by eating; taking with food or after food significantly reduces efficacy
side_effects: Long-term risks (>12 months): C. difficile infection (2× risk), community-acquired pneumonia, hip/wrist/spine fractures (reduced calcium absorption), Vitamin B12 deficiency, hypomagnesaemia (magnesium deficiency — risk of arrhythmia at severe levels), renal disease (interstitial nephritis — rare), possible dementia association (contested)
Fundic gland polyps — benign; common in long-term PPI users; no malignant potential
medicines.duration: Use for shortest appropriate duration; review indication at every consultation; many patients initiated on PPIs during hospital admission continue unnecessarily for years — 'medication inertia'
medicines.deprescription: When stopping long-term PPIs — taper over 2-4 weeks to avoid rebound acid hypersecretion (which can cause worsening heartburn — temporarily makes patient think they still need the PPI); reduce to every other day → stop

medicines.name: Pantoprazole
medicines.dosage: Dyspepsia/GERD: 40 mg once daily before breakfast; IV: 40-80 mg for bleeding peptic ulcer
medicines.use_case: Widely used alternative to omeprazole; slightly fewer drug interactions (less CYP2C19 interaction than omeprazole — preferred in patients on clopidogrel); very widely prescribed in India; IV pantoprazole for acute upper GI bleeding from peptic ulcer
medicines.iv_use: IV pantoprazole infusion (80 mg bolus + 8 mg/hour for 72 hours) — standard of care after endoscopic haemostasis for peptic ulcer bleeding (high-risk stigmata: visible vessel or clot); reduces re-bleeding risk from 22% to 7%

medicines.name: Esomeprazole
medicines.form: Tablet (20 mg, 40 mg); Granules for oral suspension
medicines.dosage: GERD: 20-40 mg once daily; erosive oesophagitis: 40 mg once daily for 4-8 weeks
medicines.use_case: The S-isomer of omeprazole; marginally superior to omeprazole for healing erosive oesophagitis in some studies; good for severe GERD; granule formulation useful for nasogastric tube administration; higher cost than generic omeprazole
medicines.note: Brand name 'Nexium' extensively marketed but evidence for significant clinical superiority over generic omeprazole at equivalent doses is limited; generic omeprazole is equally effective for most indications

medicines.name: Rabeprazole
medicines.dosage: Dyspepsia/GERD: 20 mg once daily
medicines.use_case: PPI component of H. pylori eradication (may be slightly superior to omeprazole for eradication due to less CYP2C19 polymorphism-dependent metabolism — more consistent acid suppression across different metaboliser types); GERD, peptic ulcer
medicines.note: Less affected by CYP2C19 genetic polymorphism — relevant for CYP2C19 poor metabolisers and in Asian populations where poor metaboliser frequency is higher

medicines.name: Lansoprazole
medicines.dosage: Dyspepsia/GERD: 15-30 mg once daily
medicines.use_case: GERD, peptic ulcer, H. pylori eradication; available as dispersible tablet (useful for patients with dysphagia or via nasogastric tube)

categories.purpose: Block histamine H2 receptors on gastric parietal cells, reducing gastric acid secretion. Less potent than PPIs (reduce acid by ~70% vs ~98% for PPIs) but faster onset, useful for PRN (as-needed) use, and appropriate for milder acid-related symptoms. Tolerance (tachyphylaxis) develops with continuous use within 2-3 weeks.

medicines.name: Famotidine
medicines.dosage: Dyspepsia/GERD: 20 mg twice daily or 40 mg once daily at night; PRN use: 10-20 mg as needed
medicines.use_case: Mild-moderate GERD and dyspepsia; excellent safety profile; no significant drug interactions; preferred H2 blocker for PRN (as-needed) use; safe in pregnancy and renal impairment (dose reduction in severe renal failure); OTC available in many countries for PRN heartburn
medicines.mechanism: Competitive H2 receptor antagonist on parietal cells; reduces histamine-stimulated acid secretion; faster onset than PPIs (30-60 min) but shorter duration (8-12 hours); does not significantly affect CYP enzymes
medicines.advantage_over_ppi: Faster onset of action; appropriate for breakthrough symptoms in GERD despite PPI; no significant rebound on discontinuation; better safety profile for short-term use
medicines.note: Ranitidine — previously the most widely used H2 blocker — was voluntarily withdrawn globally in 2020 due to contamination with NDMA (N-Nitrosodimethylamine — a probable human carcinogen); famotidine and cimetidine are the remaining approved H2 blockers

medicines.name: Cimetidine
medicines.dosage: 400-800 mg twice daily or 800 mg at night
medicines.use_case: Peptic ulcer, GERD; now less preferred due to significant drug interactions (strong CYP inhibitor — affects warfarin, theophylline, phenytoin, metformin, and many others); anti-androgenic effects at high doses (gynaecomastia); older generation H2 blocker
medicines.note: Significant drug interactions limit use; famotidine preferred

categories.purpose: Neutralise gastric acid on contact — providing rapid, short-lived symptomatic relief of heartburn, acid regurgitation, and mild dyspepsia. NOT curative — do not heal ulcers or eradicate H. pylori; appropriate for immediate symptom relief and mild, intermittent dyspepsia.

medicines.name: Aluminium Hydroxide + Magnesium Hydroxide Combination
medicines.dosage: 10-20 mL liquid or 2-4 tablets after meals and at bedtime (maximum 4 times daily); chew tablets — do not swallow whole
medicines.use_case: Immediate relief of heartburn, acid regurgitation, and dyspepsia; most widely used OTC antacid in India; the aluminium hydroxide component tends to cause constipation, the magnesium hydroxide causes a mild laxative effect — the combination is designed to be bowel habit-neutral; Mucaine also contains oxethazaine (surface anaesthetic — provides additional pain relief from inflamed oesophageal mucosa)
medicines.mechanism: Aluminium and magnesium hydroxides react with hydrochloric acid (HCl) to form aluminium chloride, magnesium chloride, and water — directly raising gastric pH; onset of action: 5-15 minutes; duration: 1-2 hours
medicines.limitations: Short duration of action; must be taken frequently; aluminium hydroxide binds dietary phosphate in gut (reduces phosphate absorption — concern in long-term use; may cause hypermagnesaemia in renal failure)
medicines.note: Antacids significantly reduce absorption of many medications — must be separated by at least 2 hours from: fluoroquinolones (ciprofloxacin), tetracyclines, iron supplements, levothyroxine, and bisphosphonates

medicines.name: Calcium Carbonate (CaCO3)
medicines.dosage: 500-1000 mg (1-2 tablets) after meals as needed
medicines.use_case: Fast-acting antacid with acid-neutralising and calcium supplementation benefit; often combined with magnesium carbonate for balanced bowel effects; widely available OTC
medicines.note: Calcium carbonate can cause constipation with frequent use; acid rebound possible with large doses

medicines.name: Sodium Bicarbonate (Baking Soda — Eno, Citrosoda)
brand_examples: ENO (fruit salt — sodium bicarbonate + citric acid)
medicines.dosage: ½-1 teaspoon in water or as directed on packaging; as needed
medicines.use_case: Immediate rapid relief of bloating, gas, and heartburn; very popular home remedy in India; ENO (sodium bicarbonate + citric acid) produces CO2 on dissolving — temporarily relieves gas and bloating sensation; rapid onset
medicines.caution: High sodium content — avoid in hypertension, heart failure, renal disease, or patients on sodium restriction; CO2 produced may cause belching (temporary gas relief) but also worsens GERD by increasing intragastric pressure
medicines.note: Not suitable for long-term use; high sodium content; acid-rebound can occur

medicines.name: Sucralfate (Cytoprotective Agent)
medicines.dosage: 1 g four times daily (1 hour before meals and at bedtime) or 2 g twice daily on an empty stomach
medicines.use_case: Peptic ulcer healing (particularly gastric ulcer); oesophagitis; NSAID-gastropathy; stress ulcer prophylaxis in ICU patients; forms a protective paste that adheres to ulcer base preventing acid penetration; safe in pregnancy
medicines.mechanism: Polyanionic aluminium salt — binds to positively charged proteins in ulcer crater; forms protective viscous coat over ulcer protecting from acid and pepsin; stimulates prostaglandin secretion and mucus production (cytoprotection)
medicines.note: Must be taken on an empty stomach (acid activates sucralfate); reduces absorption of fluoroquinolones, digoxin, warfarin — separate by 2 hours; rarely used in modern practice superseded by PPIs but valuable in pregnancy and where PPIs not tolerated

categories.purpose: Accelerate gastric emptying and improve coordinated GI motility — used for gastroparesis, postprandial distress syndrome (PDS), and nausea-dominant dyspepsia.

medicines.name: Domperidone
medicines.dosage: 10-20 mg three times daily 15-30 minutes before meals (maximum 30 mg/day; use lowest effective dose for shortest time)
medicines.use_case: Postprandial nausea and vomiting in dyspepsia; gastroparesis; domperidone promotes coordinated antroduodenal contractions and accelerates gastric emptying; preferred prokinetic in patients who cannot tolerate metoclopramide (fewer CNS side effects as domperidone does not cross the blood-brain barrier significantly)
medicines.mechanism: Dopamine D2/D3 receptor antagonist in GI tract and chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ); antiemetic and prokinetic; does NOT significantly cross blood-brain barrier (unlike metoclopramide) — fewer extrapyramidal side effects
side_effects: QT prolongation — most important cardiac side effect; dose-dependent and more common at higher doses and in elderly; check ECG before prescribing in high-risk patients; avoid with QT-prolonging drugs
Galactorrhoea (milk production outside pregnancy) and gynaecomastia — hyperprolactinaemia from limited D2 blockade at pituitary (outside blood-brain barrier)
medicines.caution: EMA and MHRA (2014): limit to 10 mg three times daily (or 30 mg/day total); use for maximum 1 week for acute nausea/vomiting; cardiac risk with higher doses; avoid in patients with liver impairment, electrolyte disturbances, or cardiac disease
medicines.india_note: One of the most widely prescribed drugs in India, often in combination with PPIs (e.g., Nexpro-D, Pantop-D, Rabec-DSR); frequently overused; reassess regularly

medicines.name: Metoclopramide
medicines.dosage: 10 mg orally, IV, or IM three times daily (15-30 minutes before meals); maximum 0.5 mg/kg/day
medicines.use_case: Gastroparesis (IV/IM most effective); nausea and vomiting from any GI cause; enhances gastric emptying; antiemetic; broadly useful in acute dyspeptic episodes particularly when vomiting predominates
medicines.mechanism: Central and peripheral dopamine D2 antagonist AND 5-HT4 agonist — prokinetic (enhances acetylcholine release); antiemetic (CTZ D2 blockade); CROSSES blood-brain barrier significantly — causes CNS effects
side_effects: Extrapyramidal reactions — ACUTE DYSTONIA (particularly young women and children; oculogyric crisis — eyes deviated upward; torticollis — neck twisted; opisthotonus — arched back): treat with IV/IM benztropine or procyclidine or diazepam; common and distressing
Tardive dyskinesia — irreversible involuntary movements with prolonged use (months); risk increases with total cumulative dose
medicines.caution: Maximum 5 days continuous use (FDA 2009 black box warning: prolonged use causes irreversible tardive dyskinesia); avoid in children under 18 years for dyspepsia (EMA guidance); use short-term only; ondansetron preferred as antiemetic

medicines.name: Itopride
medicines.dosage: 50 mg three times daily before meals; or 150 mg once daily (OD formulation)
medicines.use_case: Functional dyspepsia with predominant postprandial fullness and early satiety; gastroparesis; widely used in India for chronic dyspepsia with motility component; dual mechanism combines prokinetic and antiemetic benefits with a better safety profile than metoclopramide (lower CNS effects)
medicines.mechanism: D2 receptor antagonist AND acetylcholinesterase inhibitor — dual mechanism enhances gastric motility without significant CNS dopamine blockade (lower extrapyramidal risk than metoclopramide); does not significantly cross blood-brain barrier
medicines.evidence: RCTs: itopride significantly reduces FD symptoms (fullness, early satiety, upper abdominal discomfort) vs placebo; comparable to domperidone

medicines.name: Mosapride
medicines.dosage: 5 mg three times daily before meals
medicines.use_case: Functional dyspepsia; GERD (improves LOS tone and gastric emptying); postprandial fullness; widely used in India and Asia for functional GI disorders; highly selective 5-HT4 agonist with no D2 antagonism — no extrapyramidal or cardiac QT effects
medicines.mechanism: Selective 5-HT4 (serotonin type 4) receptor agonist in GI tract — stimulates enteric nervous system to enhance acetylcholine release and GI peristalsis; accelerates gastric and intestinal transit; no cardiac or CNS effects
medicines.note: Probably the safest prokinetic currently available for long-term use in functional dyspepsia

medicines.name: Erythromycin (Low-Dose) — Motilin Receptor Agonist for Gastroparesis
medicines.dosage: Gastroparesis (IV): 1-3 mg/kg IV every 8 hours (prokinetic dose — much lower than antibiotic dose); oral: 125-250 mg three times daily
medicines.use_case: Severe gastroparesis — particularly useful IV for acute gastroparesis or before procedures; erythromycin at low (subantimicrobial) doses acts as a powerful motilin receptor agonist — stimulating strong gastric antral contractions and markedly accelerating gastric emptying
medicines.mechanism: Motilin receptor agonist — mimics the hormone motilin which triggers powerful migrating motor complexes (MMC — gastric 'housekeeping' contractions) during fasting; dramatically accelerates gastric emptying
medicines.limitation: Tachyphylaxis develops rapidly (receptor desensitisation) within days of continuous use — limiting long-term utility; useful short-term for acute gastroparesis or to facilitate gastric emptying for procedures

medicines.name: Simethicone (Dimethicone)
medicines.dosage: Adults: 40-80 mg after meals and at bedtime; Infants: 20-40 mg with each feeding
medicines.use_case: Symptomatic relief of gas, bloating, and flatulence in dyspepsia and functional gut disorders; commonly included in combination antacid preparations in India; infant colic
medicines.mechanism: Silicone polymer — surface tension reducer (anti-foaming agent); causes small gas bubbles in GI tract to coalesce into larger bubbles that can be expelled more easily; does NOT reduce gas production — only facilitates its expulsion
medicines.note: Does not affect gas production or absorption — purely symptomatic gas-relief agent; safe in pregnancy and infants; no drug interactions

categories.purpose: Used for refractory functional dyspepsia not responding to acid suppression, H. pylori eradication, and prokinetics — targeting visceral hypersensitivity and gut-brain axis dysregulation through central and peripheral mechanisms. Small doses are used for their pain-modulating and GI effects — NOT for psychiatric indications (explain this clearly to patients).

medicines.name: Amitriptyline (Low-Dose TCA)
