medicines.dosage: Start: 10 mg at bedtime; titrate slowly every 2-4 weeks up to 25-50 mg at bedtime if needed; DO NOT use antidepressant doses (150+ mg) for dyspepsia
medicines.use_case: Refractory functional dyspepsia — particularly epigastric pain syndrome (EPS) with visceral hypersensitivity; not responding to PPI or H. pylori eradication; evidence: ACTIGAST trial (Talley et al., BMJ 2015) — amitriptyline 50 mg significantly improved adequate relief in FD vs placebo (particularly in EPS subtype); also useful for nausea and sleep disturbance in FD
medicines.mechanism: Tricyclic antidepressant — at LOW doses: blocks visceral afferent pain signalling (peripheral and central); 5-HT reuptake inhibition; anticholinergic effect reduces gastric secretion and slows transit (may help crampy pain); antihistaminic (sedating — beneficial at night for sleep disruption from pain)
side_effects: Cardiac arrhythmia risk at higher doses (QTc prolongation)
medicines.patient_explanation: Explain explicitly: 'This medication is being used at a very low dose specifically to reduce the sensitivity of the nerves in your stomach that are over-signalling pain — not for depression. The dose is much lower than psychiatric doses.'

medicines.name: Mirtazapine
medicines.dosage: 7.5-15 mg at bedtime (start low; increase if needed)
medicines.use_case: Functional dyspepsia with: significant nausea, weight loss, poor appetite, early satiety; mirtazapine is the only neuromodulator with evidence specifically for nausea, nausea-related weight loss, and impaired gastric accommodation in FD; also improves sleep (highly sedating); 5-HT3 antagonism (antiemetic effect); appetite stimulation
medicines.mechanism: NaSSA (noradrenaline and specific serotonin antidepressant); 5-HT3 and 5-HT2 antagonist; H1 antagonist (sedation, appetite stimulation); alpha-2 antagonist; antiemetic, anxiolytic, orexigenic (appetite stimulant), antidepressant
side_effects: Significant sedation (take at bedtime; use as advantage for sleep)
Weight gain and increased appetite (desired effect in weight-losing FD patients)

medicines.name: Buspirone
medicines.dosage: 5-10 mg three times daily
medicines.use_case: Functional dyspepsia with impaired gastric accommodation — buspirone acts on gastric fundic 5-HT1A receptors promoting fundic relaxation (accommodation); evidence: RCT by Tack et al. (Clinical Gastroenterology and Hepatology 2012) — buspirone significantly improved meal-related symptoms (fullness, early satiety, nausea) vs placebo in FD
medicines.mechanism: 5-HT1A partial agonist — in the gastric fundus, 5-HT1A receptor activation promotes nitrergic-mediated fundic relaxation (accommodation to food); anxiolytic (serotonergic) at the CNS level
medicines.note: Primarily used as anxiolytic in most markets; being repurposed for FD accommodation disorder; well tolerated; not sedating; no dependence potential

medicines.name: Escitalopram / Low-dose SSRIs
medicines.dosage: 5-10 mg daily (low dose for FD — start at 5 mg)
medicines.use_case: Functional dyspepsia with prominent anxiety or depression component; SSRIs may improve FD symptoms via central modulation of gut-brain axis; may help with co-morbid anxiety improving somatisation and amplification of GI symptoms
medicines.note: Evidence for SSRIs specifically in FD is weaker than for TCAs; use when anxiety/depression is a prominent comorbidity

categories.category_name: NSAID Gastroprotection — Prevention of NSAID-Induced Ulcer
categories.purpose: All patients requiring chronic NSAID therapy for conditions such as osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, or chronic pain must have gastroprotection assessed — a critically important preventive measure particularly in India where NSAID use is extremely common and often without gastric protection.

risk_stratification.high_risk: Previous peptic ulcer or GI bleeding; age >65; high-dose NSAID; concurrent anticoagulant, corticosteroid, or antiplatelet; serious comorbidity — MUST have PPI
risk_stratification.low_risk: No risk factors — PPI not mandatory but consider

medicines.name: PPI (Omeprazole, Pantoprazole) + NSAID combination
medicines.dosage: Omeprazole 20 mg or Pantoprazole 20-40 mg once daily taken WITH ongoing NSAID
medicines.use_case: Gastroprotection for all high-risk or moderate-risk NSAID users; reduces NSAID-induced peptic ulcer complications by ~75%
medicines.note: Must be continued for AS LONG AS NSAID is continued; not just initial prescription

medicines.name: Misoprostol (Prostaglandin E1 analogue)
medicines.dosage: 200 mcg four times daily with food
medicines.use_case: NSAID gastroprotection; cytoprotective — replaces prostaglandins depleted by COX-1 inhibition; prevents NSAID-induced gastric and duodenal ulcers; equivalent efficacy to PPIs for gastroprotection
side_effects: Diarrhoea and abdominal cramps (most common — affects compliance)
Uterotonic — ABSOLUTE CONTRAINDICATION in pregnancy (risk of miscarriage and preterm labour)
medicines.note: Poor tolerability from GI side effects; largely superseded by PPIs which are better tolerated and easier to prescribe

medicines.name: COX-2 Selective NSAIDs (Celecoxib — Celebrex)
medicines.dosage: 100-200 mg once or twice daily
medicines.use_case: Patients requiring NSAID therapy with high GI risk — COX-2 selective inhibition spares COX-1 (which protects gastric mucosa) — significantly less GI ulceration and bleeding than non-selective NSAIDs; cardiovascular safety similar to non-selective NSAIDs at equivalent doses
medicines.note: Still requires PPI addition in very high GI risk patients (prior ulcer history, anticoagulant use); contraindicated in significant cardiac disease (all NSAIDs increase CV risk)

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Dietary management is foundational in dyspepsia — many patients achieve significant symptom improvement through dietary modifications alone, without requiring medication. However, dietary triggers are highly individual — what worsens symptoms in one patient may not affect another. The approach should be PERSONALISED and based on a careful symptom diary identifying individual triggers. In Indian dietary culture, specific foods, cooking methods, spice levels, eating patterns, and meal timing are all critical considerations. The gut-brain axis means that eating under stress, eating rapidly, and irregular meal patterns are as important as food choice.

dietary_principles.meal_size_and_frequency: MOST IMPORTANT dietary change — small, frequent meals (5-6 small meals per day instead of 2-3 large meals) dramatically reduces dyspepsia for most patients. Large meals distend the stomach, trigger the gastrocolic reflex, increase acid output, and overwhelm impaired gastric accommodation. Half-fill the stomach at each meal — the stomach should never feel completely full.
dietary_principles.eating_speed: Eat slowly and chew thoroughly — rapid eating leads to aerophagia (swallowing air), poor mechanical digestion, and overwhelms the stomach's grinding function; take at least 20 minutes per meal; put the fork down between bites
dietary_principles.meal_timing: Regular meal times — avoid skipping meals (an empty stomach produces acid that irritates the mucosa); last meal at least 2-3 hours before bedtime (prevents nocturnal acid reflux and gastroparesis-related symptoms); avoid eating at irregular or very late hours
dietary_principles.posture_after_eating: Remain upright for at least 1-2 hours after eating; avoid lying down immediately after meals (allows gravity to keep stomach contents down); sleeping position: elevate head of bed by 15-20 cm using bed blocks or use a foam wedge pillow (better than adding extra pillows — pillows collapse and fold the abdomen)

recommended_foods.category: BRAT-like Bland Diet During Symptom Flares

items.benefit: Easily digestible; low fat; minimal acid production; calming for inflamed gastric mucosa; easily tolerated during acute dyspepsia flares; rice water (kanji) soothes irritated stomach lining
items.frequency: Main staple during flares; small portions every 3-4 hours

items.food: Moong dal (Yellow split mung bean) — khichdi
items.benefit: Most easily digestible legume; low in gas-producing oligosaccharides (unlike chana, rajma, urad dal); excellent protein without gas; anti-inflammatory properties; traditional Indian 'get well' food with very strong logic — combines easily digestible protein and carbohydrate in soft, non-irritating form; a small amount of ghee aids fat-soluble vitamin absorption and provides gut lining protection

Natural antacid properties (contains pectin which thickens the mucous membrane layer in the stomach — providing a protective coating against acid); potassium; easily digestible; no gastric acid stimulation; particularly useful for dyspepsia and peptic ulcers

Probiotics (Lactobacillus acidophilus, L. bulgaricus) reduce H. pylori colonisation density and improve GI mucosal health; alkaline buffering reduces gastric acidity; easily digestible protein; lactic acid promotes mucosal healing; fresh curd (not sour) is particularly soothing; the cooling effect (sheetala guna in Ayurveda) is also relevant
items.frequency: 1-2 small bowls of fresh, unsweetened curd daily — not on empty stomach; at room temperature (cold curd may trigger GERD in sensitive individuals)

items.examples: Lauki (bottle gourd), tinda (round gourd), turai (ridge gourd), carrots, sweet potato, pumpkin, beans (French beans — not rajma)
items.benefit: Gentle on stomach; low acid, low gas; lauki is particularly recommended in Ayurveda for pitta (acidic) conditions — contains cooling properties, high water content, anti-inflammatory compounds; alkalinising
items.frequency: Daily as vegetable component of meals

recommended_foods.category: Herbal and Traditional Remedies with Scientific Evidence
recommended_foods.rationale: Several traditional Indian herbal remedies for 'gas and acidity' have legitimate pharmacological mechanisms supported by evidence; these are appropriate as adjuncts or first-line for mild-moderate dyspepsia

items.benefit: 6-gingerol and shogaols: (1) Prokinetic — accelerates gastric emptying (clinically comparable to metoclopramide in some studies); (2) Anti-nausea — 5-HT3 antagonism (same mechanism as ondansetron); (3) Anti-inflammatory — inhibits COX and 5-LOX; (4) H. pylori inhibition (in vitro); (5) Reduces postprandial fullness and early satiety in FD patients (clinical evidence). One of the most evidence-based herbal interventions for dyspepsia.
items.preparation: Fresh ginger (½-1 inch piece) in 200 mL boiling water for 5-10 minutes; adrak chai (ginger tea); ginger powder capsules (500 mg-1 g twice daily); add to food during cooking
items.frequency: 1-3 cups of ginger tea daily; particularly effective 15-30 minutes before meals to stimulate gastric motility

items.benefit: Thymol (the active component of ajwain essential oil) — powerful antispasmodic, carminative (relieves gas), and digestive stimulant; reduces intestinal spasm; anti-H. pylori activity (thymol has bactericidal properties against H. pylori at high concentrations); widely used in traditional Indian medicine for indigestion, gas, bloating, and colic; one of the most evidence-supported traditional Indian digestive remedies
items.preparation: ½ teaspoon of ajwain seeds chewed raw or with black salt after meals (most traditional method); OR boiled in water to make ajwain water (ajwain ka pani); OR dry-roasted ajwain with rock salt
items.frequency: After each main meal; ajwain water sip before meals as digestive stimulant

items.benefit: Anethole (main constituent of fennel essential oil) — antispasmodic (relaxes intestinal smooth muscle — relieves cramping and spasm); carminative (reduces gas production and facilitates expulsion); anti-inflammatory; mild acid-buffering; fennel reduces intestinal spasm and relieves bloating; widely available and culturally accepted in India (served after meals in restaurants)
items.preparation: ½ teaspoon of dry-roasted saunf after meals (extremely common Indian tradition — now supported by evidence); saunf tea (1 tsp saunf in boiling water, steeped 5-10 min); fennel seed decoction
items.frequency: After each meal; particularly after heavy or spicy meals

items.benefit: Active compounds: cuminaldehyde and cymene — stimulate salivary and digestive enzyme secretion; carminative (reduces gas); improves fat digestion (stimulates lipase enzyme secretion); anti-H. pylori activity in vitro; jeera water is one of India's most widely used home remedies for 'gas and stomach problems' — now with scientific backing
items.preparation: 1 teaspoon of jeera seeds boiled in 1 glass of water for 5-10 minutes; strain; sip warm throughout the day; alternatively soak jeera overnight and drink the soaking water in the morning
items.frequency: 1-2 glasses of jeera water daily; particularly effective in the morning on empty stomach and before meals

items.benefit: Combination of three fruits: (1) Amla (Emblica officinalis): Vitamin C, antioxidant, gastroprotective, anti-H. pylori; (2) Bibhitaki (Terminalia bellirica): antispasmodic, laxative, anti-inflammatory; (3) Haritaki (Terminalia chebula): prokinetic (stimulates GI motility), anti-H. pylori, astringent. Evidence: triphala significantly reduces constipation and overall dyspeptic symptoms in clinical trials; improves gastric motility; reduces H. pylori density
items.preparation: 1-2 g Triphala powder (½ tsp) in warm water at bedtime; Triphala tablets available
items.caution: Mild laxative effect — start with ¼ tsp and increase gradually

items.benefit: Near-isotonic natural electrolyte solution; gentle on inflamed gastric mucosa; alkalinising effect on urine and mild gastric buffer; potassium, magnesium; reduces dehydration from vomiting; cooling and soothing; particularly useful when vomiting limits fluid intake
items.frequency: 1-2 glasses daily; helpful during acute dyspeptic episodes

items.food: Licorice root (Mulethi — Glycyrrhiza glabra) — DGL form preferred
items.benefit: Deglycyrrhizinated licorice (DGL) has been studied in peptic ulcer disease — stimulates mucus secretion in stomach (cytoprotective), anti-H. pylori activity (inhibits H. pylori urease), anti-inflammatory, promotes ulcer healing; evidence from multiple small RCTs showing DGL comparable to antacids for dyspepsia symptom relief
items.preparation: DGL (deglycyrrhizinated licorice) tablets or chewable — standard extract (DGL removes glycyrrhizin which causes hypertension and fluid retention in whole licorice); chew before meals
items.caution: Only use DGL form — whole licorice can cause hypertension and hypokalaemia from glycyrrhizin; DGL is safe

recommended_foods.category: Foods and Drinks That Buffer and Soothe Gastric Acid

items.benefit: Initially buffers gastric acid (momentary relief from proteins and calcium); traditional Indian remedy for acidity; however: NOTE that milk protein and calcium subsequently STIMULATE gastric acid secretion (protein is a potent acid secretagogue) — providing only short-term relief followed by rebound acid; use in moderation for acute relief, not as a long-term strategy
items.note: Cold milk is particularly popular in India for acidity; warm milk may be marginally more effective; very cold milk may worsen GERD by increasing LOS relaxation

items.benefit: Papain enzyme (proteolytic — helps digest proteins, reducing gastric workload); alkalinising; high water content; reduces postprandial discomfort; mild prokinetic effect in some studies; Vitamin C; gently soothing for inflamed gastric mucosa

items.food: Aloe vera juice (fresh, inner gel — diluted)
items.benefit: Anti-inflammatory polysaccharides (acemannan) — reduces gastric mucosal inflammation; anti-H. pylori activity in vitro; antacid-like buffering; promotes healing of eroded gastric mucosa; RCT: aloe vera syrup significantly reduced GERD symptoms; widely available in India
items.preparation: 30 mL fresh aloe vera inner leaf gel (avoid outer latex — laxative) diluted in 200 mL water; drink before meals
items.caution: Use only inner gel (aloin in outer layer is a harsh laxative); do not use in pregnancy (uterotonic in large amounts)

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Capsaicin (active compound in chillies) activates TRPV1 (transient receptor potential vanilloid 1) nociceptors in the gastric mucosa — directly stimulating pain signalling, increasing mucosal sensitivity, and worsening visceral hypersensitivity in FD; also stimulates gastric acid secretion; worsens GERD by relaxing lower oesophageal sphincter. However: capsaicin DESENSITISES TRPV1 with chronic regular exposure (explains why those accustomed to very spicy food tolerate it — they have 'tachyphylaxis' of TRPV1 receptors). For patients with dyspepsia: reduce chilli gradually; extreme avoidance may paradoxically increase TRPV1 sensitivity upon re-exposure.
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Gradually reduce (not suddenly eliminate) chilli levels; use non-chilli spices (cumin, coriander, turmeric — anti-inflammatory) instead for flavour

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.food: Fatty and Fried Foods (Tele Hua Khana)
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Dietary fat is the most potent trigger of delayed gastric emptying (fat slows gastric emptying dramatically); high-fat foods also relax the lower oesophageal sphincter (LOS) causing GERD; fat stimulates cholecystokinin (CCK) release which inhibits gastric emptying; fatty meals trigger postprandial fullness, early satiety, and nausea; deep-fried foods (samosas, pakoras, bhature, puri) are the most common dyspepsia triggers in the Indian diet
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Replace deep-frying with steaming, baking, or shallow frying in minimal oil; reduce ghee and butter in cooking; avoid heavy rich curries during flares

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.food: Tea and Coffee (Chai aur Coffee) — Excessive Consumption
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Caffeine: stimulates gastric acid secretion (parietal cell activation); relaxes lower oesophageal sphincter (worsens GERD); increases gastric motility (can worsen cramping); dehydrating (diuretic effect). Tannins in strong black tea: astringent, reduce digestive enzyme activity. Chai (Indian spiced tea with milk): the milk buffers some acidity and the spices (ginger — beneficial) modify effects; strong chai on empty stomach is a very common Indian dyspepsia trigger
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Limit to 1-2 cups of tea/coffee per day; avoid on empty stomach; add milk; prefer weak chai with ginger; never drink strong black tea or espresso on empty stomach; switch to herbal teas (ginger, fennel, chamomile)

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Carbon dioxide gas in fizzy drinks distends the stomach; increases intragastric pressure causing GERD; acid (phosphoric acid in cola; citric acid in lemonade) directly irritates oesophageal mucosa; high sugar content promotes osmotic gastric distension; the combination of acid + gas + sugar worsens dyspepsia significantly
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Avoid carbonated beverages entirely during active dyspepsia; replace with plain water, coconut water, jeera water, or herbal tea

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Direct gastric mucosal irritant (disrupts gastric mucosal barrier); stimulates gastric acid secretion; delays gastric emptying; relaxes lower oesophageal sphincter (causing GERD); worsens gastroparesis; promotes H. pylori virulence; impairs gastric mucosal healing; heavy alcohol use causes haemorrhagic gastritis and Mallory-Weiss tears (longitudinal mucosal tears at gastro-oesophageal junction from forceful vomiting after drinking)
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Complete abstinence is ideal during active dyspepsia; during maintenance: limit to very moderate intake (if at all); always take with food; avoid on empty stomach

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.food: Large, High-Fat Meals — Particularly Late at Night
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Large meals overwhelm gastric capacity and motility; fat delays gastric emptying; late-night large meals result in full stomach during sleep (highest GERD risk); nocturnal acid exposure most damaging to oesophageal mucosa; late-night heavy Indian meals (biryani, dal makhani, butter chicken at 10 PM) are a common and important dyspepsia trigger
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Dinner should be the lightest meal of the day; eat by 7-8 PM if possible; maximum 2-3 hours before bedtime; small, easily digestible dinner

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.food: Raw Onions and Garlic (Raw form — not cooked)
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Raw onions contain fructooligosaccharides (FOS) which are fermented by colonic bacteria producing gas; raw garlic and onion can directly irritate gastric mucosa in sensitive individuals; both relax the lower oesophageal sphincter; COOKED onion and garlic are generally well tolerated and have anti-inflammatory benefits (including anti-H. pylori for garlic)
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Use cooked onion and garlic in food; avoid raw in salads during flares

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.food: Certain Pulses and Legumes — Urad Dal, Rajma, Chole
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Contain raffinose, stachyose, and verbascose (non-digestible oligosaccharides) — fermented by colonic bacteria producing copious gas (hydrogen, methane, CO2); urad dal (black lentil) is particularly gas-forming and is a common trigger of bloating and flatulence; rajma (kidney beans) and chole (chickpeas) also highly gas-forming
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Soak overnight and discard soaking water before cooking (reduces oligosaccharide content by 50-70%); add ajwain or hing (asafoetida) during cooking (reduces gas production); replace with moong dal (lowest gas-producing legume) during flares; cook very well

foods_to_limit_or_avoid.food: Eating Under Stress or While Rushing
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.reason: Stress activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and sympathetic nervous system — directly impairs gastric accommodation, delays gastric emptying, increases visceral sensitivity, and reduces mucosal blood flow; eating rapidly increases aerophagia; stress eating promotes overeating; the gut-brain axis is bidirectional — psychological stress profoundly disrupts gastric function
foods_to_limit_or_avoid.recommendation: Eat in a calm, relaxed environment; no screens during meals; sit for meals; mindful eating practices; even 2-3 slow deep breaths before eating activates the parasympathetic nervous system and improves digestive function

sample_meal_plan.principle: Small, frequent, low-fat, easily digestible meals; no skipping meals; last meal 2-3 hours before bed; ajwain, saunf, ginger incorporated
sample_meal_plan.early_morning_6_to_7_am: Warm water with honey and lemon (activates digestive system gently); 1 glass jeera water (soaked overnight); 1 amla (Vitamin C, antioxidant)
sample_meal_plan.breakfast_8_am: Small bowl of soft oats/daliya with milk OR moong dal khichdi (soft); weak ginger chai with milk; 1 ripe banana; eat slowly in seated position
sample_meal_plan.mid_morning_10_am: Saunf water (fennel tea); small quantity of dry roasted chivda or 2-3 plain biscuits; ajwain water
sample_meal_plan.lunch_12_to_1_pm: Small portion plain rice + moong dal + lauki or tori sabzi (low-gas vegetable, minimal oil and spice) + small bowl fresh curd; chew saunf (fennel) after meal; walk slowly for 5-10 minutes after eating
sample_meal_plan.afternoon_3_to_4_pm: Small portion of papaya or ripe banana; ginger tea or coconut water
sample_meal_plan.dinner_6_to_7_pm: Small bowl of khichdi or plain rice + dal + steamed vegetable + minimal spice and oil; avoid heavy creamy/fatty/spicy preparation; chew ajwain after meal
sample_meal_plan.bedtime_routine: No food after 8-9 PM; warm milk with turmeric (haldi doodh) if hungry; head elevation while sleeping

weight_management.overview: Obesity is the single most modifiable lifestyle risk factor for GERD and dyspepsia. Abdominal adiposity increases intra-abdominal pressure — mechanically pushing gastric contents upward against the lower oesophageal sphincter; obesity is associated with delayed gastric emptying, impaired gastric accommodation, hiatus hernia (5× more common in obese patients), and increased acid exposure time.
weight_management.targets: Target BMI 18.5-25 kg/m2; waist circumference <90 cm (men), <80 cm (women — Indian-specific cutoffs); even 5-10% weight loss in obese dyspepsia patients significantly reduces GERD severity and frequency
weight_management.strategies: Aerobic exercise; portion control; low-fat, high-fibre diet; behavioural weight management programme

smoking_cessation.reason: Smoking worsens dyspepsia through multiple mechanisms: nicotine relaxes the lower oesophageal sphincter (promotes GERD); smoking reduces bicarbonate secretion in the duodenum (impairs duodenal defence); impairs mucosal healing; increases gastric acid output; worsens H. pylori infection severity and reduces eradication success rates; smoking is a significant risk factor for peptic ulcer disease and gastric cancer
smoking_cessation.cessation_strategies: Varenicline (Champix) first-line; NRT patches + gum; avoid bupropion in patients with active peptic ulcer (rare seizure risk); smoking cessation improves dyspepsia significantly within weeks of quitting

stress_management_and_gut_brain_axis.overview: The gut-brain axis is central to functional dyspepsia pathophysiology — psychological stress is a known trigger and perpetuating factor for FD. The vagal nerve provides bidirectional communication between the brain and enteric nervous system; CRF (corticotropin-releasing factor) secreted during stress directly delays gastric emptying and increases visceral hypersensitivity. Addressing psychological factors is essential for refractory FD.
strategies: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy (CBT) — the most evidence-based psychological treatment for functional GI disorders; CBT addresses catastrophising, symptom hypervigilance, and maladaptive illness behaviours; available individually or in group format; 8-12 sessions typically recommended

Gut-directed hypnotherapy — very strong evidence for IBS and emerging evidence for FD; hypnosis specific to gut function reduces visceral hypersensitivity and improves gastric accommodation; multiple RCTs support benefit
Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction (MBSR) — reduces stress-related gastric hyperacidity; improves gut-brain signalling; 8-week programme
Progressive muscle relaxation and diaphragmatic breathing — directly activates the parasympathetic nervous system, suppressing stress-induced gastric hypersecretion and motility dysfunction
Regular aerobic exercise — reduces anxiety and depression (gut-brain); improves gastric motility and transit; reduces bloating; even 20-30 minutes of brisk walking improves GI symptoms

Yoga and pranayama — Specific yoga poses (Pawanmuktasana — wind-releasing pose; Uttanpadasana; Vajrasana — sitting on heels after meals: a traditional Indian practice shown to improve gastric emptying and reduce postprandial discomfort; Balasana — child's pose; gentle abdominal twists) promote GI motility and reduce gas accumulation; Pranayama (diaphragmatic breathing) reduces sympathetic tone
Biofeedback therapy — for supragastric belching (a specific belching disorder requiring behavioural retraining); reduces aerophagia

positional_and_lifestyle_modifications_f: Elevate head of bed by 15-20 cm using bed blocks or foam wedge — reduces nocturnal oesophageal acid exposure; more effective than using extra pillows (which flex the abdomen increasing intra-abdominal pressure)

Sleep on LEFT side — reduces GERD (anatomy: lying on left side positions the gastro-oesophageal junction above the gastric pool of acid — reduces acid reflux into oesophagus); lying on right side worsens GERD
Remain upright for minimum 1-2 hours after meals; avoid lying down; a gentle walk (10-15 minutes) after meals improves gastric emptying and reduces reflux
Avoid tight clothing and tight waistbands — increases intra-abdominal pressure worsening GERD
Avoid exercise immediately after large meals — intense exercise diverts blood away from GI tract and increases intra-abdominal pressure; exercise ≥2 hours after meals
h_pylori_hygiene_prevention: Clean water — drink only filtered, boiled, or bottled water in areas with uncertain water quality; H. pylori is waterborne
Proper handwashing — soap and water for ≥20 seconds before eating and after toilet; H. pylori spreads fecal-orally
Food hygiene — wash fruits and vegetables; avoid street food prepared with uncertain water quality during outbreaks
Avoid sharing utensils, drinking vessels, or pre-chewing food for children (common in some Indian households) — H. pylori oral-oral transmission
Test and treat family members if one member has H. pylori and peptic ulcer disease — H. pylori clusters in families

green_zone.status: Mild Dyspepsia — No Alarm Features — Home/OTC Management
green_zone.criteria: Symptoms <3 times per week; no alarm features; <6 months duration in age <55; identifiable dietary triggers; responds to antacids; no weight loss
green_zone.action: 4-week trial of lifestyle modification + OTC antacids or H2 blocker; food and symptom diary; reduce NSAIDs if in use; reassess at 4 weeks — if not improving, see GP

yellow_zone.status: Moderate Dyspepsia — GP Review — Test and Treat
yellow_zone.criteria: Symptoms ≥3 days per week; not responding to OTC management; significantly affecting quality of life; no alarm features; age <55
yellow_zone.action: GP assessment; H. pylori urea breath test or stool antigen test; if H. pylori positive — eradicate (14-day triple or quadruple therapy); if H. pylori negative — empirical PPI 4-8 weeks (omeprazole 20 mg once daily); review medications (NSAID use); referral if no response after 8 weeks

red_zone.status: ALARM FEATURES — URGENT 2-WEEK-WAIT REFERRAL FOR ENDOSCOPY
criteria: Age ≥55 years with new onset dyspepsia
Sudden severe epigastric pain with rigid abdomen — possible perforation — EMERGENCY SURGERY
red_zone.action: For haematemesis/melaena/perforation: CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES IMMEDIATELY (102/112). For other alarm features: urgent gastroenterology referral for 2-week-wait upper GI endoscopy; blood tests (FBC, LFTs, ferritin); CT imaging if mass suspected

follow_up_monitoring.h_pylori_eradication: Confirm eradication with UBT or stool antigen at minimum 4 weeks after completing antibiotics (2 weeks off PPIs); if eradication confirmed and symptoms resolved — no further routine investigation required; if symptoms persist — functional dyspepsia management
follow_up_monitoring.ppi_therapy_review: Reassess at 4-8 weeks; if responding, consider step-down or PPI holiday; do not continue PPIs indefinitely without documented indication; annual review of PPI prescription
follow_up_monitoring.long_term_monitoring: Patients with confirmed peptic ulcer: endoscopy to confirm healing (especially gastric ulcer — mandatory biopsy and healing confirmation at 6-8 weeks); patients with severe oesophagitis or Barrett's oesophagus — surveillance endoscopy as per gastroenterology guidelines

complications.complication: Peptic Ulcer Disease (Gastric or Duodenal Ulcer)
complications.description: The most important complication of untreated H. pylori gastritis and unprotected NSAID use. Full-thickness mucosal defect penetrating through the muscularis mucosae. Can cause: chronic pain; GI haemorrhage (20% of peptic ulcers); perforation (5%); gastric outlet obstruction (pyloric stenosis — 2%).
complications.severity: Moderate to Severe (pain, anaemia); Life-threatening (haemorrhage, perforation)
complications.management: H. pylori eradication (heals 95% of DU without recurrence); PPI 4-8 weeks; stop NSAIDs; endoscopy to confirm healing of gastric ulcers (mandatory biopsies)

complications.description: Life-threatening complication of peptic ulcer disease — rupture of a blood vessel in the ulcer base. Haematemesis (vomiting fresh blood or coffee-ground material) and melaena (black, tarry, foul-smelling stools from digested blood — at least 50-100 mL of blood in upper GI tract). Mortality 10% overall; higher in elderly, comorbid patients, and large bleeds.
complications.management: EMERGENCY — call 102/112; IV access × 2; IV fluid resuscitation; urgent upper GI endoscopy (OGD) for diagnosis and haemostasis (injection, thermal coagulation, haemostatic clips, Hemospray); IV PPI (pantoprazole 80 mg bolus + 8 mg/hour infusion for 72 hours post-haemostasis); H. pylori eradication; stop all NSAIDs; blood transfusion; surgical or radiological (angio-embolisation) intervention for failed endoscopic haemostasis

complications.description: Full-thickness perforation of the gastric or duodenal wall — allows GI contents to spill into the peritoneal cavity causing generalised peritonitis. Presents as SUDDEN, SEVERE, 'worst ever' epigastric pain — the patient describes it as 'like something tearing' or 'like being stabbed'; the abdomen becomes board-like rigid (peritonism). Perforation is a surgical emergency — mortality 10-15% if treated within 12 hours, rising rapidly with delay.
complications.management: EMERGENCY surgery; nil-by-mouth; IV antibiotics; IV fluids; erect chest X-ray or CT scan (free air under diaphragm = perforation); emergency laparoscopic or open repair (Graham patch — omentum patching the perforation hole)

complications.description: The most feared long-term complication of untreated chronic H. pylori infection and the final common pathway of the Correa cascade (H. pylori gastritis → chronic atrophic gastritis → intestinal metaplasia → dysplasia → gastric adenocarcinoma). Gastric cancer is the 5th most common cancer globally and 3rd leading cause of cancer death. H. pylori causes 89% of non-cardia gastric cancers. In India: gastric cancer is more common in southern India (especially Kerala, Karnataka) and northeastern states. Early gastric cancer is curable; advanced gastric cancer has poor prognosis.
complications.prevention: H. pylori eradication significantly reduces gastric cancer risk (particularly in pre-malignant gastritis stages); benefits greatest when eradicated before atrophic gastritis develops; mass eradication programmes are being debated as public health intervention in high-prevalence countries

complications.description: Metaplastic change in the distal oesophageal epithelium from normal squamous to specialised intestinal-type columnar epithelium (goblet cells) — a consequence of chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux (GERD). Barrett's oesophagus is a precancerous condition — 0.3-0.5% per year risk of progression to oesophageal adenocarcinoma. Detected on endoscopy and confirmed by biopsy. Requires endoscopic surveillance every 3-5 years (longer interval for non-dysplastic Barrett's); 2-yearly for low-grade dysplasia; immediate treatment for high-grade dysplasia.
complications.severity: Moderate (premalignant) — requiring surveillance; High (oesophageal adenocarcinoma) — if untreated
complications.management: PPI therapy (reduces acid exposure — may slow progression); endoscopic surveillance; radiofrequency ablation (RFA) for dysplastic Barrett's — highly effective (>90% complete eradication of dysplasia)

complications.complication: Nutritional Deficiencies from Long-Term PPI Use
complications.description: Chronic PPI therapy (>12 months) significantly impairs absorption of several micronutrients: (1) Vitamin B12 — gastric acid is required to liberate B12 from food proteins; PPI use causes food-cobalamin malabsorption (crystalline cyanocobalamin in supplements is still absorbed — dietary B12 is the problem); B12 deficiency causes megaloblastic anaemia, peripheral neuropathy, and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. (2) Magnesium — severe hypomagnesaemia with PPI use (rare but potentially fatal arrhythmia); check Mg in patients on long-term PPIs developing tetany, seizures, or arrhythmia. (3) Iron — gastric acid required for ferric-to-ferrous conversion (absorption-ready form). (4) Calcium — reduced calcium absorption increases fracture risk with long-term PPI.
complications.severity: Mild to Moderate (usually) — serious if neurological B12 deficiency missed
complications.management: Annual FBC and B12 in long-term PPI users (>12 months); B12 supplementation if deficient (cyanocobalamin 1000 mcg/day oral is effective even without intrinsic factor); check Mg in those on PPIs with muscle cramps or arrhythmia

complications.complication: Psychological Burden and Quality of Life Impact
complications.description: Chronic dyspepsia — particularly functional dyspepsia — significantly impairs quality of life (comparable to other chronic conditions like inflammatory bowel disease and diabetes in some measures). Anxiety and depression are both causes and consequences of FD — the gut-brain axis is bidirectional. The impaired quality of life manifests as: reduced ability to socialise (food-centered social activity avoidance); work impairment (from pain and fatigue); sleep disruption; sexual dysfunction; and significant healthcare utilisation. Untreated psychological comorbidity perpetuates the chronic pain cycle.
complications.management: Screen for depression and anxiety (PHQ-9, GAD-7); CBT; gut-directed hypnotherapy; low-dose neuromodulators; gastroenterology-psychology liaison

key_points: Dyspepsia and heartburn are EXTREMELY common in pregnancy — affecting 60-80% of pregnant women; the most frequent GI complaint in pregnancy

Causes: progesterone (relaxes lower oesophageal sphincter — direct pharmacological mechanism); relaxin (loosens GI smooth muscle); growing uterus displacing and compressing the stomach (particularly third trimester); delayed gastric emptying from progesterone; elevated oestrogen worsening nausea
Management — pregnancy-safe first: small, frequent meals; avoid trigger foods; head elevation; left lateral decubitus position; weight gain within recommended limits

Safe antacids in pregnancy: calcium carbonate (Tums — also provides calcium supplementation); magnesium hydroxide (after first trimester — avoid large amounts near delivery); aluminium hydroxide (short-term OK, avoid long-term — Al toxicity concerns)
H2 blockers in pregnancy: Famotidine — limited safety data but widely used in second/third trimester; preferred over PPIs if antacids insufficient

PPIs in pregnancy: omeprazole and esomeprazole — generally considered safe based on large registry data; use only if H2 blockers insufficient and symptoms severe; avoid in first trimester if possible (limited data)

AVOID in pregnancy: misoprostol (abortifacient); bismuth subsalicylate; domperidone (limited data); metoclopramide (first trimester — limit to short-term use for severe nausea/vomiting; Category B in USA)

H. pylori in pregnancy: test and treat can be delayed until after delivery — H. pylori eradication antibiotics (clarithromycin, tetracycline) are not recommended in pregnancy; bismuth contraindicated; amoxicillin is safe in pregnancy but not used in single agent treatment; DEFER H. pylori eradication until postpartum

Hyperemesis gravidarum: severe, intractable nausea and vomiting causing >5% weight loss, ketonaemia, and dehydration in pregnancy; requires hospitalisation; IV ondansetron; IV fluids; metoclopramide; thiamine supplementation
Prevalence of organic dyspepsia (peptic ulcer, gastric cancer) is significantly higher in the elderly — lower threshold for investigation

NSAID use is more common in elderly (osteoarthritis, cardiovascular aspirin) — NSAID-induced gastropathy is the leading cause of dyspepsia in elderly; ALWAYS check NSAID use; add PPI if NSAIDs necessary
Age ≥55 years with NEW onset dyspepsia is an ALARM FEATURE — mandatory endoscopy
Alarm features may be subtle or absent in elderly patients with gastric cancer (anorexia, anaemia, weight loss); maintain high index of suspicion

Polypharmacy in elderly: multiple medications causing dyspepsia simultaneously (NSAIDs + corticosteroids + bisphosphonates + iron + metformin + antibiotics); medication review is diagnostic and therapeutic
H. pylori eradication in elderly: same regimens, same outcomes; important to prevent peptic ulcer complications; check antibiotic interactions with other medications
PPI use in elderly: be aware of side effects (C. difficile, fractures, B12 deficiency, hypomagnesaemia) — particularly important with polypharmacy; review indication at every prescription
Dysphagia in elderly: new dysphagia is NEVER a normal feature of ageing — always investigate (Zenker's diverticulum, oesophageal web, cancer, motility disorder)
Gastroparesis is very common in longstanding type 1 and type 2 diabetes (30-50%) — a specific and underdiagnosed complication of diabetic autonomic neuropathy affecting the vagus nerve

Gastroparesis presents as: postprandial nausea, vomiting of undigested food hours after eating, severe early satiety, weight loss, and erratic blood glucose control (food absorption is unpredictable causing glycaemic swings)
Diagnosis: 4-hour solid gastric emptying scintigraphy — the gold standard; recommended in all diabetics with unexplained vomiting or difficult glycaemic control

Management: optimise glycaemia (acute hyperglycaemia directly inhibits gastric motility); dietary modification (low-fat, small, frequent liquid/semi-liquid meals); prokinetics (metoclopramide IV for acute; domperidone or mosapride oral for maintenance); erythromycin short-term; consider gastric electrical stimulation (Enterra device) for severe refractory gastroparesis

SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) — recently recognised to delay gastric emptying; consider contribution to gastroparesis symptoms; GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide) also significantly delay gastric emptying
Metformin GI side effects: nausea, diarrhoea, metallic taste — very common on initiation; switch to extended-release (XR) formulation to reduce GI intolerance significantly; take with food
15-30% of chronic NSAID users develop peptic ulcers; 1-2% per year experience serious complications (haemorrhage, perforation)

Risk stratification essential: HIGH RISK (must have PPI gastroprotection): age >65; prior peptic ulcer or GI bleed; high-dose NSAID; concurrent corticosteroids or anticoagulants; significant comorbidity

Test for H. pylori before starting long-term NSAID therapy — H. pylori + NSAID combination has multiplicative (not additive) risk for peptic ulcer complications; eradicate H. pylori before continuing NSAID
Lowest effective NSAID dose for shortest duration; regular reassessment of NSAID need
COX-2 selective NSAID (celecoxib) reduces GI risk by 50% vs non-selective NSAIDs; still requires PPI in very high-risk patients
Topical NSAIDs (diclofenac gel) for localised pain — significantly lower systemic GI risk than oral NSAIDs
Paracetamol: preferred over NSAIDs for mild-moderate pain in patients at GI risk — no direct gastric mucosal toxicity

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 2-dose series (0 and 6-18 months); lifelong protection after both doses
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Hepatitis A causes acute hepatitis with jaundice and elevated liver enzymes that mimics severe dyspepsia in the pre-icteric phase. More importantly, patients with pre-existing chronic liver disease (cirrhosis, hepatitis B/C) who develop superimposed HAV have very high risk of fulminant hepatic failure. All patients with chronic dyspepsia from any cause who have chronic liver disease or are immunocompromised should be vaccinated. Also important for food handlers (dyspepsia is a common occupational health issue in food service workers).
vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: Vaccinate all patients with chronic liver disease; food handlers; international travellers

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Influenza infection frequently causes GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain) that exacerbate underlying dyspepsia; influenza illness triggers NSAID and aspirin use for myalgia and fever — worsening drug-induced gastropathy; annual influenza vaccination reduces illness burden and reduces the need for pain-related NSAID use in dyspepsia patients
vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: Annual vaccination for all patients with significant comorbidities or in whom influenza-related NSAID use would be harmful

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: Primary series and boosters per national schedule
vaccinations_recommended.reason: COVID-19 causes significant upper GI symptoms (nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhoea) in 30-40% of infected individuals and can exacerbate chronic dyspepsia. Post-COVID GI symptoms (functional dyspepsia, IBS-like symptoms) are recognised in Long COVID syndrome. COVID-19 infection triggers increased NSAID and analgesic use, worsening drug-induced gastropathy in susceptible patients.
vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: Follow national vaccination schedule; important for those with co-existing GI comorbidities

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: 2-dose (Rotarix) or 3-dose (RotaTeq) oral series from 6 weeks of age
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Rotavirus gastroenteritis in infancy can trigger post-infectious functional dyspepsia and IBS in childhood and adulthood. Post-infectious FD after childhood viral gastroenteritis has been documented — early prevention of severe rotavirus may reduce lifetime functional GI disorder burden.
vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: Universal infant vaccination per national immunisation schedule

when_to_see_doctor: Dyspepsia not improving after 4 weeks of lifestyle changes and OTC antacids — GP review required
Any alarm feature present — same-day or urgent medical evaluation: unexplained weight loss, dysphagia, persistent vomiting, iron deficiency anaemia, blood in stools
Haematemesis (vomiting blood, even a small amount) — EMERGENCY; call 102/112 immediately
Black tarry stools (melaena) — possible upper GI bleeding — EMERGENCY
New or changed dyspepsia in anyone over 55 years — endoscopy required; do not wait
Dyspepsia persisting despite 8 weeks of PPI treatment — referral for endoscopy and gastroenterology evaluation
Family history of gastric or oesophageal cancer with new dyspepsia symptoms at any age
Severe or rapidly worsening epigastric pain — possible peptic ulcer, pancreatitis, or biliary colic — same-day evaluation
Sudden severe 'worst ever' epigastric pain with abdomen becoming rigid — possible peptic ulcer perforation — EMERGENCY surgery
Diabetic patient with worsening nausea and vomiting of undigested food — possible gastroparesis — needs gastric emptying study
Dyspepsia starting or worsening after beginning a new medication (especially NSAIDs, aspirin, steroids, bisphosphonates, metformin, iron) — discuss medication change with prescriber
Dyspepsia in a patient with known chronic liver disease (hepatitis B/C, cirrhosis) — any new GI symptoms can indicate complications; do not delay
Confirmed H. pylori infection — needs eradication therapy and test of cure; do not leave untreated
Pregnant woman with severe, persistent vomiting affecting nutrition — hyperemesis gravidarum — GP or obstetric team same day
emergency_signs: Haematemesis — vomiting fresh red blood or dark coffee-ground material — upper GI haemorrhage from peptic ulcer or varix — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES (102/112) IMMEDIATELY; IV access, blood transfusion, urgent endoscopy required
Melaena — black, tarry, foul-smelling stools — upper GI bleeding — EMERGENCY; even in the absence of vomiting blood — call 102/112

Sudden severe epigastric pain — the worst pain of their life; described as 'tearing', 'knife-like', or 'explosion' — with abdominal rigidity (board-like abdomen) — POSSIBLE PEPTIC ULCER PERFORATION — EMERGENCY SURGERY; call 102/112
Severe vomiting leading to severe dehydration — rapid heart rate (>120 bpm), dry mouth, not passing urine, extreme weakness — EMERGENCY IV fluids needed

Confusion or altered consciousness in a patient with known chronic liver disease who presents with worsening GI symptoms — possible hepatic encephalopathy from GI haemorrhage precipitating decompensation — EMERGENCY
Iron deficiency anaemia in a patient over 55 years with dyspepsia — possible gastric cancer — urgent endoscopy within 2 weeks
Progressive dysphagia (worsening difficulty swallowing) over weeks — possible oesophageal or gastric cancer — urgent 2-week referral for endoscopy
Rapidly deteriorating general condition with epigastric pain, fever, and rigidity — possible peritonitis from perforated ulcer — EMERGENCY
Severe constant epigastric pain radiating to the back with elevated serum lipase — possible acute pancreatitis — EMERGENCY hospitalisation

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the difference between indigestion, acidity, gas problem, and GERD?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: These terms are often used interchangeably in India but have distinct medical meanings: 'Indigestion' (dyspepsia) is an umbrella term for upper abdominal discomfort — including fullness, early satiety, pain, bloating, and nausea — originating from the stomach and duodenum. 'Acidity' colloquially refers to the burning sensation from gastric acid — this can be from GERD (reflux into the oesophagus) or from gastric acid irritating the stomach lining. 'Gas problem' (vayu problem) describes bloating, excessive belching, and flatulence from gas in the upper GI tract — often from swallowed air (aerophagia) or fermentation. 'GERD' (Gastro-oesophageal Reflux Disease) is specifically the condition where acid from the stomach flows backward into the oesophagus — causing heartburn (burning behind the breastbone) and acid regurgitation (sour taste in the mouth). In practice, these conditions frequently overlap and a patient may have elements of all four — careful history-taking helps distinguish the dominant problem.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is H. pylori and why is it so important in India?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) is a bacterium that lives in the stomach lining — infecting approximately 70-80% of people in India, usually acquired in childhood through contaminated water and food. It causes chronic inflammation of the stomach (gastritis) in everyone infected, though most people have no symptoms. H. pylori is critically important because it is: the primary cause of peptic ulcers (stomach and duodenal ulcers); a WHO Group 1 carcinogen — the most important preventable cause of gastric cancer; and a major contributor to iron deficiency anaemia. The good news: it can be completely detected with a simple 15-minute urea breath test and cured with a 10-14 day course of two antibiotics and a PPI (acid-reducing medication). After H. pylori eradication, peptic ulcers heal without recurrence in 95% of patients, and gastric cancer risk significantly decreases.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Should I take a PPI (acid tablet like omeprazole or pantoprazole) every day for my acidity?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: PPIs (proton pump inhibitors like omeprazole, pantoprazole, esomeprazole) are excellent for treating acid-related conditions — but only when genuinely needed, at the lowest effective dose, for the shortest appropriate duration. Unfortunately, in India, PPIs are among the most overused and over-prescribed medications — many people take them daily for years without any documented indication. Long-term daily PPI use is not harmless — it can cause: Vitamin B12 deficiency (leading to anaemia and nerve damage), magnesium deficiency (muscle cramps, arrhythmia), increased risk of C. difficile diarrhoea, reduced calcium absorption (increased fracture risk), and possible kidney and cognitive effects. PPIs are appropriate for: active peptic ulcer (4-8 weeks); GERD with oesophagitis (ongoing); H. pylori eradication (as part of the regimen); NSAID gastroprotection (as long as NSAID continues). If you have been on a PPI for more than 3-6 months without a documented diagnosis, ask your doctor whether you still need it — in many cases, the PPI can be safely stepped down or stopped.

frequently_asked_questions.question: My endoscopy was completely normal but I still have stomach pain and fullness. Why?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: You most likely have functional dyspepsia (FD) — a genuine disorder where the stomach is hypersensitive and has abnormal motility (the stomach muscle doesn't relax properly when food arrives or empties too slowly), even though the stomach looks structurally normal on endoscopy. Think of it like chronic back pain — a normal X-ray doesn't mean there's no pain. Functional dyspepsia is the most common cause of dyspepsia — affecting 70% of all dyspepsia patients. A normal endoscopy is actually reassuring — it means there's no cancer, ulcer, or serious structural disease. FD is best managed with: identifying and avoiding your personal food triggers (food diary); eating small, frequent meals; managing stress (the gut-brain connection is very real — psychological stress directly affects stomach sensitivity and emptying); prokinetic medications (domperidone, itopride, mosapride) if fullness and early satiety predominate; and sometimes low-dose neuromodulators (amitriptyline, mirtazapine) for refractory pain.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Are home remedies like jeera water, ajwain, saunf, and adrak chai actually helpful for indigestion?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — many traditional Indian home remedies for indigestion have well-documented pharmacological mechanisms. Ginger (adrak): contains 6-gingerol which is a natural 5-HT3 antagonist (antiemetic) and prokinetic — clinically shown to accelerate gastric emptying and reduce nausea; one of the most evidence-supported natural remedies for indigestion globally. Ajwain (carom seeds): contains thymol which is a powerful antispasmodic and carminative — relieves intestinal cramps and gas; multiple scientific studies confirm its efficacy. Saunf (fennel): contains anethole — antispasmodic, carminative, and gas-relieving; reduces intestinal smooth muscle spasm. Jeera (cumin) water: stimulates digestive enzyme secretion and has carminative properties. These remedies are not just cultural traditions — they have real pharmacological activity. For mild dyspepsia, trying these natural approaches first (along with dietary modification) is entirely reasonable before resorting to medication. They can also be used alongside prescribed medicines.

frequently_asked_questions.question: When should I be worried about my indigestion — when does it become serious?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Most indigestion is benign — it is the alarm features (red flags) that distinguish potentially serious causes. ALWAYS see a doctor urgently if you experience: (1) Vomiting blood (haematemesis) or noticing black tarry stools (melaena) — signs of GI bleeding; (2) Unexplained weight loss of >3 kg without trying — possible cancer or serious disease; (3) Increasing difficulty swallowing (dysphagia) — possible oesophageal or stomach cancer or stricture; (4) Persistent vomiting that doesn't resolve; (5) Iron deficiency anaemia without clear explanation; (6) You are over 55 years old and symptoms are new or have changed recently; (7) A family member had stomach or oesophageal cancer. Additionally: sudden severe 'worst ever' stomach pain with a rigid, board-like abdomen = possible perforated ulcer — CALL 102/112 immediately. Routine indigestion without these features is almost never serious — but if symptoms persist beyond 4-8 weeks without responding to basic treatment, a GP review is appropriate.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is the best way to sit or sleep to reduce my acid reflux at night?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Several positional strategies significantly reduce nocturnal acid reflux: (1) HEAD OF BED ELEVATION: Place bed blocks (15-20 cm) under the legs at the head of your bed — or use a foam wedge pillow beneath the mattress. This keeps the oesophagus above the stomach level using gravity to keep acid down. Simply adding extra pillows is NOT effective — it bends you at the waist, actually increasing stomach pressure; (2) SLEEP ON YOUR LEFT SIDE: Anatomy matters — on the left side, the gastro-oesophageal junction is positioned above the gastric acid pool; on the right side, the acid pool is right against the junction. Multiple studies confirm left-side sleeping significantly reduces acid reflux time and oesophageal acid exposure. (3) Do NOT eat within 2-3 hours of bedtime — your stomach needs to be at least partially empty before lying down. (4) Avoid tight pyjamas or trousers that constrict the abdomen.
